concepts.def: A **client** (a browser or an app) asks for something and a **server** does the work and answers. Almost every system in this pack is built from this one idea.
The client sends a request and waits until the server sends a response. On the canvas this is a **sync** connection: a solid line with a filled arrow.
A part whose failure takes the whole system down. It is acceptable when an outage is cheap and dangerous when it is not.
Rough arithmetic with round numbers (a day is about 86,400 seconds, 1 GB is 1,000 MB) to see whether a design is in the right order of magnitude before building it.
Split a system into a **presentation** tier (the client), an **application** tier (servers running the code) and a **data** tier (the database). Each tier talks only to its neighbour.
Stores data in tables with rows and columns, joins them in queries and keeps changes safe with transactions. The default choice for structured data.
The internet's phone book: it turns a name like `shop.example` into the IP address of the servers. Answers are cached for a **TTL**, so changes spread slowly.
Encrypts traffic between the client and the server and proves the server is who it claims to be. Usually **terminated** at a proxy or load balancer in front of the app.
A server in front of your app servers that receives every request first. It can terminate TLS, cache responses, compress and forward to the right backend.
Stores files (images, videos, backups) as objects addressed by key. Cheap, durable and nearly unlimited, but not a database: no queries, no transactions.
A server that keeps nothing about users between requests. Any instance can answer any request, so you can add, remove or restart servers freely.
Login sessions kept in a fast shared store (cache or key-value) instead of one server's memory, so every app server can see them.
Handling more load by adding more machines rather than a bigger machine. Needs stateless servers and something to spread the traffic.
Work that runs outside the user's request: reports, emails, clean-ups. A scheduler or queue starts it and a worker does it.
An HTTP call a partner makes **to you** when something happens (a payment succeeded). Providers retry on failure, so the same webhook can arrive more than once.
An operation is idempotent when doing it twice has the same effect as doing it once. It makes retries safe: a repeated "mark order 42 paid" changes nothing.
A small backend built for one kind of client (web, mobile, TV) that shapes responses exactly for it, while shared services stay generic.
Creating IDs that never collide, even when many servers create them at once: counters handed out in ranges, random IDs, or time-based IDs.
Read-only copies of a database kept up to date by **replication**. They take read traffic off the primary; all writes still go to the primary, and replicas can lag slightly behind.
Copying every change from one database to others. **Synchronous** replication waits for the copy (safer, slower); **asynchronous** doesn't (faster, may lose the latest writes on failure).
How many reads happen for each write. Read-heavy systems benefit from replicas and caches; write-heavy ones need stores built for fast writes.
Stores a value under a key and fetches it by that key, very fast. No joins or complex queries — which is exactly what lets it scale easily.
Stores records as JSON-like documents that don't all need the same fields. Good for data whose shape varies; weaker at joins across documents.
Stores nodes and the relationships between them, and walks relationships quickly ("friends of friends"), where SQL needs a join per hop.
Built for measurements stamped with a time: fast appends, range queries and rollups, and cheap compression of old data.
Splitting one dataset across several databases by a **shard key**, so each holds a part of the data and a part of the load.
A way to map keys to shards so that adding or removing a shard moves only a small share of the keys, instead of nearly all of them as with `hash % N`.
Many app servers share a small, reused set of database connections through a pooler, because each database connection costs memory and the database allows only so many.
A time-limited link that lets a client upload or download one object directly from storage, without giving it credentials and without passing the bytes through your servers.
Hot storage is fast and pricier, cold and archive tiers are cheap but slow to read. **Lifecycle rules** move objects down the tiers as they age.
Keeping a copy of frequently read data in fast memory so most reads skip the slower store. Every cache has to answer: what happens when the data changes?
The app reads the cache first and loads from the database on a miss, then fills the cache. The cache never talks to the database itself.
A content delivery network keeps copies of files and pages in data centres close to users, so most requests never travel to your servers.
Every write goes to the cache and the database together before it is confirmed, so the cache is never stale — at the price of slower writes.
Writes land in the cache and are flushed to the database later in batches. Very fast writes; the risk is losing unflushed data if the cache dies.
When a hot key expires, thousands of requests miss at once and all hit the database. Fixed by letting one request refill while others wait or get the stale value.
A compact bit array that answers "definitely not here" or "maybe here". Lets you reject lookups for keys that don't exist without touching the database.
Caching the answer "not found" for a short time, so repeated requests for missing keys stop reaching the database.
Many keys expiring at the same moment (for example, all loaded at startup with the same TTL), flooding the database. Random jitter on TTLs spreads the expiries out.
How long a cached copy is considered fresh. Longer TTLs mean fewer misses and staler data.
What a full cache throws out: **LRU** drops the least recently used item, **LFU** the least frequently used. LFU protects items that are always popular from one-off scans.
Caching whole responses of public GET endpoints at a proxy or CDN, controlled by headers like `Cache-Control`, so identical requests never reach the app.
Spreading requests over several servers with an algorithm (round robin, least connections, hashing) and **health checks** that stop sending traffic to broken servers.
The load balancer regularly asks each server "are you OK?" and stops routing to any that fail, so a crash becomes invisible to users.
**L4** balances TCP connections without reading them — fast and good for long-lived connections. **L7** reads HTTP, so it can route by path, header or cookie.
The load balancer sends a user to the same server every time. Convenient for stateful apps, but load becomes uneven and a server failure still loses sessions.
Adding and removing servers automatically based on load, between a minimum (for safety) and a maximum (for cost). New servers take minutes to start, so it follows trends, not instant spikes.
Capping how many requests a client can make in a time window (token bucket, leaky bucket, sliding window). With many gateways the counters must be shared.
DNS that answers with the nearest (or fastest) region's address, so users in each continent are served locally.
One shard or key receives far more traffic than the rest (a celebrity, a viral product), so adding shards doesn't help. Fixed with caching the hot key or splitting it.
When work arrives faster than it can be done, a bounded queue pushes back and the front door rejects excess requests early, instead of everything slowing down until it collapses.
A long-lived two-way connection between client and server, so the server can push messages instantly. Each open connection holds memory on a gateway.
A publisher sends a message to a topic and every subscriber receives a copy. Senders don't need to know who is listening.
Separate data centres inside one region, with independent power and network. Spreading copies across zones survives one zone failing.
Stopping two transactions from changing the same data at once. **Pessimistic** locking locks the row first; **optimistic** locking checks a version number at write time and retries on conflict.
A buffer where producers leave jobs and workers take them one at a time. It decouples the two sides, smooths bursts and lets you add workers when the backlog grows.
Answering the user right away and doing slow work (emails, resizing, reports) afterwards in the background.
Where messages go after failing too many times, so one bad message can't block the rest. Someone inspects them and replays or discards them.
Several workers read from the same queue; each message goes to exactly one of them. Throughput grows with the number of workers.
An append-only, replayable log of events split into partitions. Consumers track their own position and can re-read history.
Order is kept only within a partition. Choosing the partition key (for example account ID) keeps each account's events in order while different accounts run in parallel.
Workers sharing a group split a stream's partitions between them; different groups each receive all events independently.
A message that becomes visible only after a set time — a simple way to run something "in 24 hours" without a cron job per item.
How long a stream keeps events. With enough retention, a new consumer can start from the beginning and rebuild its data from history.
**At-most-once** may lose messages; **at-least-once** never loses but may duplicate. "Exactly once" in practice means at-least-once plus idempotent processing.
Remembering the IDs of messages or requests already handled, so a redelivered one is recognised and skipped.
Uploaded media flows through storage, a queue and workers that transcode it into several formats, then back to storage and out through a CDN.
Queues where urgent messages (a password reset) are delivered before bulk ones (a newsletter), so floods of low-priority work don't delay what matters.
Running more than one of everything that matters — load balancers, servers, databases — in different failure domains, so one failure is absorbed instead of felt.
Switching traffic from a failed component to its standby. Automatic failover needs health checks and something that decides; manual failover needs a runbook and time.
The maximum time a caller waits for an answer. Without one, a hung dependency ties up threads until the caller itself falls over.
Retrying a failed call after waiting longer each time (**exponential backoff**) with a random offset (**jitter**), so thousands of clients don't retry in lockstep and flatten a recovering service.
After too many failures, the caller stops calling a dependency for a while and fails fast (or uses a fallback), giving the dependency room to recover.
Serving a simpler answer when a dependency fails — cached, default or partial content — so the core of the product keeps working.
Isolating resources (queues, worker pools, connection pools) per kind of work, so one flooded workload can't starve the others — like watertight compartments in a ship.
Rejecting some requests on purpose when overloaded — lowest priority first — so the rest are served well instead of everything timing out.
**RPO** is how much data you may lose (time since the last good copy); **RTO** is how long recovery may take. Backups must be stored away from what they protect and restores must be tested.
**Active-passive** keeps a standby region ready to take over. **Active-active** serves traffic in several regions at once and must resolve conflicting writes.
When two regions change the same record at once, something must decide the result: last write wins, merging rules, or data types built to merge (CRDTs).
Saving an event in an **outbox table** in the same transaction as the business change, and publishing it afterwards with a relay, so the two can never diverge.
A user always sees their own latest changes, even if other users may briefly see older data. Often done by reading from the primary for a short time after a write.
Copies may disagree for a while, but if writes stop they all converge to the same value. Cheap and available; the application must tolerate stale reads.
With **N** copies, a write waits for **W** acknowledgements and a read asks **R** copies. If **R + W > N**, every read overlaps the latest write.
Several instances agree that exactly one of them is the leader and does the work; if it dies, another is elected. Built on a consistent coordination service.
A lock held in a coordination service (with a lease that expires) so that processes on different machines don't change the same thing at once.
A coordinator asks every database to **prepare**, then tells all to **commit** (or all to abort). Atomic across databases, but blocking if the coordinator fails mid-way.
A long business transaction split into local steps, each with a **compensating** step that undoes it if a later step fails. No global lock; consistency is eventual.
Services react to each other's events with no central controller. Loosely coupled, but the overall flow exists only implicitly.
A central orchestrator tells each service what to do next and tracks the state of the whole process. Easy to follow and change; the orchestrator must itself be reliable.
Reading a database's change log and publishing each insert, update and delete as an event — without changing the application.
Command Query Responsibility Segregation: writes go to a model built for correctness, reads to separate **projections** built for each query, kept up to date from events.
Storing every change as an immutable entry and deriving current state from them. Nothing is updated in place, so history is a complete audit trail.
How much concurrent transactions can see of each other: read committed < repeatable read < **serializable**, which behaves as if transactions ran one at a time.
Replacing a legacy system piece by piece: a router in front sends each migrated route to the new service and everything else to the old one, until the old one can be switched off.
Each service owns its data and is the only one that reads or writes it. Others ask through its API or its events, so services can change their schema independently.
Instances register themselves in a **service registry** as they start and stop; callers look up healthy instances instead of using fixed addresses.
A **sidecar** proxy next to each service handles encryption, retries and metrics; a **control plane** configures them and issues certificates so every call uses **mutual TLS**.
Users log in once at an **identity provider**, which issues signed tokens (often JWTs) that every service can verify on its own.
A JSON Web Token: signed claims about a user that any service can verify with the issuer's public key, without calling the issuer on each request.
Passwords and API keys live in a **secrets manager**, fetched at runtime and rotated, never in code or config files. Encryption keys stay in a **KMS**.
Putting only the entry points (load balancers) in public subnets, and app servers and databases in private subnets with no inbound internet access.
**Logs** say what happened, **metrics** show how much and how fast, **traces** follow one request across services. Alerts turn signals into action.
Each request gets a **correlation ID** passed along every call; each service reports timed spans, so you can see where the time goes across services.
A single entry point for clients that routes to services and handles cross-cutting concerns: authentication, rate limits, TLS.
An **inverted index** maps each word to the documents containing it, so keyword queries with ranking, typos and filters are fast. It is a copy of the data, kept in sync from the source.
Suggestions for each keystroke, served from a precomputed prefix index and heavily cached, because every character typed is a request.
Extract data from operational databases, Transform it, Load it into a **warehouse** built for analytics, usually in scheduled batches away from production traffic.
Computing over events as they arrive — counts, sums, joins — grouped into **windows** (tumbling, sliding, session) so results are continuously up to date.
Cheap storage for raw data in any format, kept "forever" and processed later by batch jobs. Schema is applied when reading, not when writing.
A model turns text or images into vectors so that similar meanings are close together; a **vector index** finds the nearest vectors to a query.
Combining keyword search (exact terms, names, codes) with vector search (meaning), then merging the rankings, which beats either alone.
Clients send a heartbeat every few seconds; a key with a short TTL marks them online and simply expires when heartbeats stop.
Indexing positions with geohashes or quadtrees so "what is near this point?" reads a few cells instead of every location.
A **URL frontier** queue feeds fetchers; new links go back into the frontier after deduplication, with politeness limits per site and cached DNS lookups.
Keeping raw metrics for a short time and rolled-up averages for longer, so storage stays bounded while long-range charts stay fast.

concepts.term: Fan-out on write vs. on read
concepts.def: **On write**: when someone posts, copy it into every follower's timeline — fast reads, expensive for accounts with millions of followers. **On read**: assemble the timeline when it is opened. Real feeds mix both.
Video is cut into short segments in several resolutions; the player picks the best one its connection can sustain, segment by segment.
Splitting files into chunks identified by their hash, so only changed chunks are uploaded and identical chunks are stored once.
Pairing supply and demand in real time (riders and drivers, orders and couriers) from fresh location data, with each unit of supply assigned exactly once.
Holding inventory (a room, a seat) for a short time during checkout and confirming it inside a transaction or with a lock, so it can't be sold twice.
Enforcing shared limits across many gateways with counters in a fast shared store, fetched with tight timeouts and a clear rule for what happens when the store is unreachable.
Keeping each area's data in the region that serves it (a city's orders in its nearest region), so most traffic stays local and regions fail independently.
Every replica, region and managed service has a price. Good designs spend where requirements demand it and stay simple elsewhere.

challenges.title: Hello, server
challenges.brief:
A product designer wants a personal portfolio site: a home page, a handful of project pages and a contact form. Visitors open it in a web browser.

Keep it as simple as it can be. One server is fine for now — the designer would rather pay for coffee than for infrastructure.
functional: Visitors open the portfolio in a web browser
The server returns the pages
The server receives contact-form messages
nonFunctional: Pages load in under a second
Keep the running cost as low as possible

estimate.q: How much data does the site send to visitors per day?
estimate.workings: 2,000 visits × 4 pages × 500 KB = 4,000,000 KB ≈ 4,000 MB ≈ 4 GB per day.

tradeoff.q: Why is a single server a reasonable choice here?
choices: Servers never fail, so one is always enough.
The load is tiny and a short outage of a personal site is acceptable, so a second server would mostly add cost.
One server is always faster than two servers behind a load balancer.
tradeoff.why: 8,000 page views a day is about one request every 10 seconds, which one small server handles easily. A second server would buy availability, not speed — and a portfolio can live with a few minutes of downtime.

challenges.learn:
Every web system starts here: a **client** sends a request and a **server** sends back a response. One server is the cheapest and simplest design; the trade-off is that it is a **single point of failure** — when it goes down, so does the site.

Later challenges add pieces only when a requirement asks for them. Adding a database or a CDN here would work, but it costs more and solves problems this site doesn't have yet.

rules.text: Visitors use a web browser
rules.hint: Start with the person: who opens the site, and with what?

rules.text: A server answers the requests
rules.hint: Something has to run the site's code and send the pages back.

rules.text: The browser sends requests to the server
rules.hint: Draw the connection in the direction of the request: from the caller to the one being called.

rules.text: Browsers don't talk to a database directly
rules.hint: Anyone can read the code running in a browser, including database passwords. Let the server be the only one that talks to storage.

challenges.title: Remember my tasks
challenges.brief:
A small team is building a to-do app. People add tasks in the browser, tick them off, and expect to find them again tomorrow — on any device.

Today the prototype keeps tasks in the server's memory, so every restart wipes them. Make them stick.
functional: Create, complete and delete tasks
See the same tasks from any device after signing in
nonFunctional: Tasks survive server restarts
Nobody can read another person's tasks

estimate.q: How much storage do all the tasks need?

tradeoff.q: Why store tasks in a database instead of the app server's memory?
choices: Memory is too small to hold 1 GB.
A database keeps data on disk, so it survives restarts and can be shared by several servers.
Databases are always faster than memory.
tradeoff.why: 1 GB would fit in memory, and memory is faster. The reason is durability: a restart or crash empties memory, while the database writes every change to disk.

challenges.learn:
This is the **three-tier** shape you will see in almost every challenge: the client talks to the app, and only the app talks to the database.

The database adds a network hop and something else to run, but in exchange data survives restarts and several app servers can share it later.

rules.text: People use the app from a browser or phone
rules.hint: Start with who uses it.

rules.text: Requests go to an app server
rules.hint: Something has to check who is asking and run the to-do logic.

rules.text: Tasks are saved in a database behind the app
rules.hint: Memory is wiped on restart. Where do rows live safely?

rules.text: Clients don't talk to the database directly
rules.hint: Code running on a user's device can be read and changed by that user, including any database password. Let a server be the only one that talks to storage.

challenges.title: What's the address?
challenges.brief:
A bakery has bought `crumbs.example` and wants customers to type it instead of an IP address that changes whenever the hosting company moves their server.

Show how a browser finds the bakery's server and then talks to it.
functional: Customers open the site by its name
The server can move to a new IP without customers noticing
nonFunctional: Name lookups must not slow down every page view

estimate.q: With a 1-hour TTL, at most how many times a day does one visitor's resolver ask for the address?
estimate.workings: The answer is cached for 1 hour, so at most one lookup per hour: 24 hours → 24 lookups, however many pages are viewed.

tradeoff.q: The bakery plans to move servers next week. What should they do with the TTL?
choices: Raise it to one week so the address is cached longer.
Lower it (say to 5 minutes) a day before the move, then raise it again afterwards.
TTL doesn't matter; DNS changes are instant.
tradeoff.why: Resolvers keep the old address until the TTL runs out. A short TTL during the move means customers switch within minutes; a long TTL the rest of the time keeps lookups rare.

challenges.learn:
**DNS** is a lookup, not a hop in the traffic path: the browser asks DNS for the address, then connects to the server itself. That's why the arrows go browser → DNS and browser → server.

The **TTL** trades freshness for load: long TTLs mean fewer lookups but slow changes.

rules.text: A DNS service knows the site's address
rules.hint: Names have to be turned into addresses somewhere.

rules.text: The browser looks the name up
rules.hint: Who asks for the address? Draw the arrow from the one asking.

rules.text: The browser then calls the server directly
rules.hint: Once it knows the address, the browser connects to the server itself.

rules.text: DNS answers lookups; it doesn't forward traffic
rules.hint: An arrow from DNS to the server suggests requests pass through DNS. They don't: DNS only hands back an address.

challenges.title: Lock the door
challenges.brief:
A community forum is adding accounts. Right now the login form posts passwords over plain HTTP, and anyone on the café Wi-Fi can read them.

Put HTTPS in front of the forum without rewriting the app, and make sure nothing reaches the app except through that front door.
functional: Members log in with a password
All pages are served over HTTPS
nonFunctional: Passwords are never sent in clear text
Certificates are managed in one place

tradeoff.q: Why terminate TLS at a reverse proxy instead of inside the app?
choices: The app can't encrypt anything.
Certificates and ciphers are configured in one place, and the app stays simple; the proxy can also cache and compress.
Traffic behind the proxy becomes encrypted twice, which is safer.
tradeoff.why: Terminating at the proxy centralises certificates and crypto work. The trade-off: traffic between proxy and app is plain unless you re-encrypt it, so that link must stay on a private network.

challenges.learn:
A **reverse proxy** is a single front door: it holds the certificate, speaks HTTPS to the world and forwards plain requests to the app on a private network.

The front door only helps if it is the **only** door — if the app is also reachable directly, attackers simply walk around it.

rules.text: A reverse proxy handles HTTPS
rules.hint: Something in front of the app should speak HTTPS for it.

rules.text: Browsers reach the app through the proxy
rules.hint: Put the proxy between the browser and the app.

rules.text: Nothing reaches the app around the proxy
rules.hint: Is there any arrow from a browser straight to the app?

rules.text: Accounts are stored in a database
rules.hint: Password hashes have to live somewhere durable.

rules.text: Members find the forum by name
rules.hint: How does the browser learn the proxy's address?

rules.text: Clients don't talk to the database directly
rules.hint: Code running on a user's device can be read and changed by that user, including any database password. Let a server be the only one that talks to storage.

challenges.title: Heavy pictures
challenges.brief:
A recipe site lets cooks upload step-by-step photos. The first version stored the photos inside the database, and now backups take all night and the database disk is nearly full.

Keep recipes searchable and fast, but move the pictures somewhere that suits them.
functional: Cooks upload photos with each recipe
Readers see recipes with their photos
nonFunctional: The database stays small and fast to back up
Photos load quickly for readers

estimate.q: How much space do the photos take?
estimate.workings: 20,000 recipes × 10 photos × 2 MB = 400,000 MB ≈ 400 GB.

tradeoff.q: Why keep photos in object storage and only their keys in the database?
choices: Databases can't store binary data at all.
Object storage is cheap and made for large files; the database stays small, so queries and backups stay fast.
Object storage supports SQL joins on images.
tradeoff.why: Databases can store blobs, but every byte makes backups, replicas and caches heavier. Object storage costs a fraction per GB and serves files directly; the database keeps just a short key per photo.

challenges.learn:
Put each kind of data where it fits: **rows** in the database, **files** in object storage, linked by a key.

The trade-off is two places to keep consistent — if the database row is deleted, something must delete the photo too — but backups shrink from hours to minutes.

rules.text: Readers and cooks use the site through an app server
rules.hint: Recipes still need code to create and show them.

rules.text: Recipes live in a database
rules.hint: Titles, ingredients and steps are structured rows.

rules.text: Photos are kept in object storage
rules.hint: Large files belong in storage built for files.

rules.text: Photos can reach readers from storage
rules.hint: How does a photo get from storage to the reader's screen?

rules.text: Photos are served through a CDN
rules.hint: Most readers view the same popular photos. Where could copies be kept close to them?

rules.text: Clients don't talk to the database directly
rules.hint: Code running on a user's device can be read and changed by that user, including any database password. Let a server be the only one that talks to storage.

challenges.title: Two servers, one login
challenges.brief:
An online bookshop added a second app server behind a load balancer to cope with growth. Since then, customers get logged out at random and their baskets vanish.

The reason: each server remembers logins in its own memory. Fix it so any server can serve any request.
functional: Customers stay logged in while browsing
Traffic is spread over two or more app servers
nonFunctional: Any server can handle any request
Losing one server doesn't log everyone out

estimate.q: How much memory do all peak sessions need in the shared store?
estimate.workings: 8,000 sessions × 2 KB = 16,000 KB ≈ 16 MB — tiny for a cache.

tradeoff.q: Why not just turn on sticky sessions at the load balancer?
choices: Sticky sessions are not supported by load balancers.
They hide the problem: when a server dies its users still lose their sessions, and load spreads unevenly.
Sticky sessions make every request slower.
tradeoff.why: Stickiness pins a user to one server, so it works until that server restarts or gets overloaded. A shared session store removes the dependency on any one server.

challenges.learn:
Make app servers **stateless**: move anything that must outlive a request (sessions, baskets) into a shared store. Then any server can answer anyone, and you can add or restart servers freely.

The cost is one extra network call per request to the session store — usually well under a millisecond from a cache.

rules.text: A load balancer spreads requests over the app servers
rules.hint: Something must sit in front and pick a server.

rules.text: At least two app servers
rules.hint: Set replicas to 2 or more, or draw two app servers.

rules.text: App servers are stateless
rules.hint: Mark the app servers stateless once they no longer keep sessions in memory.

rules.text: Sessions live in a shared store
rules.hint: Where can every server read the same session quickly?

rules.text: The load balancer skips broken servers
rules.hint: Look at the load balancer's properties.

rules.text: Sticky sessions hide the real problem
rules.hint: With a shared session store, stickiness only makes load uneven.

challenges.title: Night shift
challenges.brief:
A chain of garden shops wants a sales summary in every manager's inbox at 6 a.m. The report scans the whole day's sales and takes several minutes to build.

The shop's web app must stay fast while this runs, and the report must still go out if nobody is awake to press a button.
functional: Build a daily sales report from the database
Email it to 40 managers every morning
nonFunctional: Runs without anyone triggering it
Doesn't slow down the checkout

estimate.q: If the report job reads each sale once, how many rows per second must it read to finish in 5 minutes?
estimate.workings: 30,000 rows / 300 s = 100 rows per second — easy for a database, but still better off the checkout path.

tradeoff.q: Why run the report in a background job instead of when a manager opens a page?
choices: Background jobs are always faster.
It runs on a schedule with nobody present, and its heavy queries stay away from customer requests.
Email can only be sent from background jobs.
tradeoff.why: Scheduled work needs something that keeps time (a scheduler) and something that does the work (a worker). Doing it inside a web request would tie up a server for minutes and depend on someone clicking.

challenges.learn:
Split **when** from **how**: a **scheduler** decides when a job starts, and a **worker** does the slow part away from user traffic.

The trade-off is more moving parts to monitor — a job that silently stops running is easy to miss, so later chapters add alerting.

challenges.title: Money's in
challenges.brief:
A concert-merch shop takes card payments through a payment provider. The provider doesn't answer immediately; it calls the shop back with a **webhook** when a payment succeeds — and if the shop doesn't answer within a few seconds, it calls again.

Last month some orders were marked paid twice and two T-shirts shipped. Design the payment flow so repeats are harmless.
functional: Customers pay at checkout
The provider notifies the shop when a payment succeeds
Paid orders are marked paid
nonFunctional: A repeated notification never changes an order twice

estimate.q: Worst case, how many webhook calls per day could arrive?
estimate.workings: 3,000 orders × (1 call + 3 retries) = 12,000 calls. Every one must be safe to repeat.

tradeoff.q: Why must the webhook handler be idempotent?
choices: Because the provider sends every webhook exactly once.
Because the provider retries when it doesn't hear back, so the same notification can arrive several times.
Because idempotent code runs faster.
tradeoff.why: Delivery over a network is "at least once": a timeout doesn't tell the provider whether you processed it. Keying the update on the payment ID makes the second call a no-op.

challenges.learn:
Webhooks turn a partner into a **client of your system**, with retries you don't control. Make the handler **idempotent** — record the payment ID and ignore ones you've seen.

The trade-off is one more lookup per call, which is far cheaper than shipping a second parcel.

challenges.title: Two clients, two needs
challenges.brief:
A local news site has a web page and a phone app. The web page shows full articles with sidebars; the app wants a compact list that loads on a slow train connection. Both teams keep changing the shared API to suit themselves and breaking each other.

Give each client its own backend while the article logic stays in one shared service.

The app shows a compact, paged list
Articles are managed in one place
nonFunctional: Mobile responses stay small
The web and app teams can ship independently

estimate.q: If one article list is 400 KB for web and the app's trimmed list is 40 KB, how much less data does the app download per list?
estimate.workings: (400 − 40) / 400 = 0.9 → 90% less data per list, which matters on a train.

tradeoff.q: What is the main cost of a backend per client?
choices: Clients become slower.
More services to build and run, and some logic may be duplicated between them.
The shared service can no longer have a database.
tradeoff.why: Each BFF is another deployable thing. The payoff is that each client team shapes its own responses without negotiating every field with the other.

challenges.learn:
A **backend for frontend** gives each client a thin layer shaped to its screen, while the domain logic lives once in a shared service.

It costs extra services and some duplication; it pays off when clients differ a lot and are built by different teams.

challenges.title: Pastebin
challenges.brief:
Developers want to paste a block of text, get a short link like `paste.example/k7Qx2`, and share it. Pastes can be up to 1 MB, most are read a few times in the first day, and they expire after a year.

The service must survive losing a server, and links must never collide.

Open a paste by its link
Pastes expire after a year
nonFunctional: Links are unique
No single app server failure takes the service down
Reads are fast

estimate.q: How much paste content is stored after one year?
estimate.workings: 1M pastes × 10 KB = 10 GB per day; × 365 days ≈ 3,650 GB ≈ 3.65 TB.

estimate.q: How many new pastes per second, on average?

tradeoff.q: Why keep paste bodies in object storage and only metadata in the database?
choices: Object storage gives each paste a short link automatically.
Bodies are large and read whole; object storage holds terabytes cheaply while the database keeps small, queryable rows.
Databases can't store text.
tradeoff.why: 3.65 TB of blobs would bloat the database and its backups. Metadata (key, owner, expiry) is tiny and needs queries, which is what the database is good at.

challenges.learn:
This combines the whole chapter: a **load balancer** over **stateless** app servers, **metadata** in a database, **blobs** in object storage, and an **ID generator** so two servers never hand out the same link.

The trade-off is more parts to run than one server with a disk — in exchange it survives a server failure and grows by adding servers.

challenges.title: Read-heavy blog
challenges.brief:
A popular cooking blog publishes a few posts a day, but readers open about a hundred pages for every comment or edit. At lunchtime the single database is at 95% CPU, almost all of it from reads.

Take the read load off the primary without changing where writes go.
functional: Readers browse posts and comments
Authors publish posts; readers post comments
nonFunctional: Reads keep working at lunchtime peaks
Writes are never lost

estimate.q: What is the average number of database reads per second?
estimate.workings: 5,000,000 page views × 10 queries / 86,400 s ≈ 579 reads/s on average (about 1,740 at a 3× peak) — posts with comment threads, author cards and sidebars add up.

tradeoff.q: What do readers risk when reads go to replicas?
choices: They may see data a moment old, because replication is usually asynchronous.
Their writes may be lost.
Replicas return random data.
tradeoff.why: Replicas trail the primary by milliseconds to seconds. For a blog, seeing a new comment a second late is fine; for a bank balance it might not be.

challenges.learn:
With a 100:1 read/write ratio, reads are the load. **Read replicas** copy the primary and serve reads, so you scale reads by adding replicas.

The trade-off is **replication lag**: a reader might briefly miss the newest write. Writes still have one home, the primary.

challenges.title: Cart in a flash
challenges.brief:
A fashion shop's cart page does a five-table join on every click and takes 400 ms. The cart is always fetched whole, by the shopper's ID, and nobody ever searches inside carts.

Make the cart instant. Orders, once placed, still need a proper relational home.
functional: Add and remove items from a cart
Load the whole cart by shopper ID
Checkout turns the cart into an order
nonFunctional: Cart reads under 10 ms
Abandoned carts don't pile up forever

estimate.q: How much data do all active carts take?
estimate.workings: 2,000,000 carts × 2 KB = 4,000,000 KB ≈ 4 GB — small enough to keep hot.

tradeoff.q: Why is a key-value store a good fit for carts?
choices: It supports complex joins across carts.
Carts are always read and written whole by one key, which is exactly the operation a key-value store makes fast and easy to scale.
It is the only store that can hold JSON.
tradeoff.why: When the access pattern is "get by ID, put by ID", a key-value store gives single-digit-millisecond lookups and scales by adding nodes. You give up ad-hoc queries you didn't need.

challenges.learn:
Choose stores by **access pattern**. Carts are fetched whole by one key, so a **key-value store** fits; orders need transactions and reports, so they stay relational.

The trade-off: two stores to operate, and checkout must copy the cart into an order carefully.

challenges.title: Shape-shifting catalog
challenges.brief:
An outdoor-gear marketplace sells tents (capacity, weight, season), boots (size, sole, waterproofing) and hundreds of other kinds of product. The SQL product table now has 300 mostly-empty columns, and every new category needs a schema migration.

Store products so each kind can have its own attributes.
functional: Sellers list products with category-specific attributes
Shoppers view product pages
nonFunctional: New categories need no schema migration
Product pages load in one read

estimate.q: If an average product document is 4 KB, how big is the catalog?

tradeoff.q: What do you give up by moving products to a document database?
choices: The ability to store numbers.
Easy joins and strict schemas: the application must validate documents and avoid cross-document transactions.
Fast reads by product ID.
tradeoff.why: Documents make varied shapes easy and keep a product in one read. In exchange, the database no longer enforces the schema and multi-document joins are awkward.

challenges.learn:
A **document database** lets each record carry the fields it needs, and returns a whole product in one read.

The trade-off is weaker guarantees: schema checks move into the app, and queries across many documents are harder than SQL joins. Orders and payments often stay relational.

challenges.title: Friends of friends
challenges.brief:
A hobby social network wants a "people you may know" box: friends of your friends, ranked by how many friends you share. In SQL the query joins the friendship table with itself three times and takes 12 seconds.

Store the relationships in a way that makes walking them fast.
functional: Store who is friends with whom
Suggest friends-of-friends ranked by mutual friends
nonFunctional: Suggestions in under 200 ms
Profiles still load quickly

estimate.q: How many friends-of-friends does one user have before removing duplicates?
estimate.workings: 300 friends × 300 friends each = 90,000 candidates — why each extra hop in SQL hurts.

tradeoff.q: Why is a graph database faster for this query?
choices: It keeps the whole dataset in the browser.
It stores each person's connections next to them, so following a hop is a pointer walk rather than a join over a huge table.
It doesn't need to read any data.
tradeoff.why: Graph databases make traversal cost depend on the neighbourhood you touch, not the size of the whole table. They are less suited to big aggregate reports, so profiles and analytics usually live elsewhere.

challenges.learn:
When the question is about **relationships** — hops, paths, neighbours — a **graph database** answers it by walking edges instead of joining tables.

The trade-off is another specialised store to keep in sync with the main user data. Caching the results helps, because suggestions don't need to be real-time.

challenges.title: Sensor flood
challenges.brief:
A greenhouse company has 50,000 sensors reporting temperature and humidity every 10 seconds through a small device app. Growers look at charts of the last day, week or year.

The current SQL table has 40 billion rows and the charts take minutes. Design the ingestion and storage.
functional: Receive readings from every sensor
Show charts per greenhouse over any time range
nonFunctional: Keep up with every reading, without gaps
Year charts load in seconds

estimate.q: How many readings arrive per second?
estimate.workings: 50,000 sensors / 10 s = 5,000 writes per second, every second of the day.

estimate.q: How much raw data per day?

tradeoff.q: What does downsampling old data trade away?
choices: Nothing; it is free.
Detail: after a while you keep one-minute or one-hour averages instead of every reading, so old spikes shorter than that disappear.
The ability to store new readings.
tradeoff.why: Year charts don't need 10-second points. Rolling old data into averages cuts storage and makes long-range queries fast, at the cost of losing fine detail.

challenges.learn:
Sensor data is **append-only and time-ordered**, and read as ranges. A **time-series database** is built for exactly that: fast appends, compression, and rollups (downsampling).

Put several ingestion servers behind a load balancer, since 5,000 writes a second never stops. The trade-off of downsampling is losing detail in old data.

challenges.title: One box isn't enough
challenges.brief:
A messaging app's user database has reached 8 TB and 400,000 queries a second. The biggest machine the cloud sells is already in use, and it is still not enough.

Split the users across several databases. The team expects to add shards every few months, so adding one must not reshuffle everyone.

Add shards as the user base grows
nonFunctional: Each shard holds a fair share of users
Adding a shard moves as few users as possible

estimate.q: With 3 shards, how much data does each hold?
estimate.workings: 400M × 20 KB = 8 TB = 8,000 GB; 8,000 GB / 3 ≈ 2,667 GB (about 2.7 TB) per shard.

tradeoff.q: You go from 3 to 4 shards. Roughly what share of users move with `hash(id) % N` versus consistent hashing?
choices: About 25% with modulo, about 75% with consistent hashing.
About 75% with modulo, about 25% with consistent hashing.
None in either case.
tradeoff.why: Changing N changes the result of `% N` for most keys, so ~3 in 4 users move. Consistent hashing moves only the keys the new shard takes over, ~1/4.

challenges.learn:
**Sharding** splits data by a **shard key** so each database holds part of it. Pick a key that spreads load evenly and that most queries include (here: user ID).

Use **consistent hashing** so growth moves only a fraction of keys. The trade-off: queries that don't include the shard key must ask every shard.

challenges.title: Too many connections
challenges.brief:
A ticketing site scaled its app tier to 40 servers for a big launch. Each server opens 50 database connections, and the database — limited to 500 — now refuses most of them with "too many clients". Adding app servers made things worse.

Let the app tier keep growing without drowning the database in connections.

nonFunctional: Total database connections stay under the limit
App servers can scale out freely

estimate.q: How many connections do the app servers try to open in total?
estimate.workings: 40 servers × 50 connections = 2,000, four times the limit of 500.

tradeoff.q: What does a connection pooler cost you?
choices: Nothing at all.
An extra hop on every query, and some session features (like session-level settings) may not work in transaction pooling mode.
The database can no longer run transactions.
tradeoff.why: The pooler multiplexes thousands of client connections onto a few hundred real ones. You pay a small latency hop and lose per-connection session state between transactions.

challenges.learn:
Database connections are expensive, and the database caps them. A **connection pooler** lets thousands of app-side connections share a small set of real ones.

The trade-off is a small extra hop and some limits on session features — well worth it once the app tier is large.

challenges.brief:
A dating app lets people upload profile photos straight from their phones. Today every photo streams through the app servers, which spend most of their CPU and bandwidth shuffling bytes, and uploads fail when a server restarts mid-transfer.

It checks who the member is, creates a short-lived signed URL, and records the photo's metadata when the upload finishes.
It receives the photo and forwards it to storage.
tradeoff.why: The server stays in charge of permission and bookkeeping; only the heavy bytes skip it. The trade-off is a two-step flow the client must follow, and cleaning up uploads that never get confirmed.

challenges.brief:
A bank must keep application logs for seven years for auditors. Engineers search the last two weeks almost daily; older logs are opened maybe twice a year, and nobody minds waiting hours for them.

All logs sit on expensive fast storage today. Keep the recent ones fast and make the old ones cheap, automatically.

tradeoff.q: What do you accept by moving old logs to an archive tier?
choices: The logs may be deleted at random.
Reading them takes hours and costs a retrieval fee, in exchange for a storage price many times lower.
Archived logs can't be read at all.
tradeoff.why: Archive tiers are cheap because data sits offline. That is fine for logs read twice a year, and wrong for anything a user waits on.

challenges.learn:
**Storage tiers** match cost to access: hot for what is read daily, cold or archive for what is kept "just in case". **Lifecycle rules** move objects down the tiers automatically.

The trade-off is slow, sometimes paid retrieval of old data — pick the tier by how long someone can wait.

A marketing team wants short links like `go.example/Ab3x` that redirect instantly and never break. Campaign links get shared millions of times, and a redirect that takes a second loses the click.

choices: It is the only store that can hold URLs.
Every redirect is a lookup by one key, and a key-value store makes that fast and scales out easily to terabytes.
It supports complex reports on clicks.
tradeoff.why: The access pattern is "get long URL by short code". A key-value (or wide-column) store serves that in milliseconds and grows by adding nodes; you don't need joins.

Estimate first: ~39 writes/s but ~3,900 reads/s and 3 TB — a **read-heavy key lookup**. That points to a **key-value store**, a **cache** for hot links, an **ID generator** to avoid collisions, and several stateless app servers behind a load balancer.

The trade-off of caching is staleness if a link is edited — acceptable for links that almost never change.

challenges.title: Cache-aside
challenges.brief:
A professional network shows a profile card next to every post. Each card needs a 30 ms database query, and the same few thousand profiles are shown over and over. The database is busy answering the same questions all day.

Add a cache the app controls: check it first, and fall back to the database on a miss.

nonFunctional: Most profile reads skip the database
The site still works if the cache is empty

tradeoff.q: What happens right after the cache restarts empty?
choices: Nothing; caches never restart.
Every read misses and goes to the database until the cache warms up again, so the database must survive that burst.
The site returns errors until someone refills the cache by hand.
tradeoff.why: Cache-aside degrades gracefully: an empty cache means slow, not broken. But the database must be able to take the full load for a while, or you need a gradual warm-up.

challenges.learn:
In **cache-aside** the app owns the logic: read the cache, on a miss read the database and fill the cache. The cache stays a simple key-value memory.

The trade-off is **staleness**: after an edit the cache may serve the old card until its TTL expires or the app deletes the key.

challenges.title: Static at the edge
challenges.brief:
A design-tools startup hosts its web app in one European region. Users in Australia wait four seconds for the first screen, almost all of it spent downloading scripts, fonts and icons that are the same for everyone.

Serve the static files from close to each user. The API can stay where it is.
functional: Load the web app's scripts, styles and images
Call the API after the app loads
nonFunctional: First screen under one second worldwide
Deploying a new version never serves a mix of old and new files

estimate.q: With a 95% hit ratio, how much static data per day still comes from your origin?
estimate.workings: 1M × 3 MB = 3 TB/day; 5% misses × 3,000 GB = 150 GB/day from the origin.

tradeoff.q: How do you use a very long CDN TTL and still ship updates instantly?
choices: Purge the whole CDN on every deploy and hope it finishes.
Put a content hash in each file name (app.3f9a.js), so a new version is a new URL and old copies simply stop being requested.
Set the TTL to zero.
tradeoff.why: Versioned file names make every file immutable, so it can be cached for a year. Only the small HTML page that points at them needs a short TTL.

challenges.learn:
A **CDN** puts copies of static files near users; your storage becomes the **origin** it fills from.

Long TTLs give high hit ratios but stale content — versioned file names get you both. Dynamic API calls still travel to your servers.

challenges.title: Live leaderboard
challenges.brief:
A mobile puzzle game shows a global top-100 after every level. Players complain that their new high score doesn't appear, because the leaderboard cache refreshes only every five minutes.

Keep the leaderboard in memory for fast reads, but make sure every score update reaches both the cache and the database before the game confirms it.
functional: Submit a score after each level
Show the top 100 and the player's own rank
nonFunctional: A new score appears on the leaderboard immediately
No confirmed score is ever lost

estimate.q: How many score writes per second?
estimate.workings: 50,000 / 60 s ≈ 833 writes/s — against 20,000 reads/s.

tradeoff.q: What does write-through cost compared with cache-aside?
choices: Reads become slower.
Every write waits for both cache and database, so writes are slower, and rarely read data also ends up in the cache.
The cache can no longer be read.
tradeoff.why: Write-through keeps the cache always fresh by paying on the write path. With 24 reads per write and a strict freshness need, that is a good deal.

challenges.learn:
**Write-through** writes to the cache and the database together, so readers never see a stale value.

You pay with slower writes. It fits read-heavy data that must be fresh, like a leaderboard; it would be wasteful for data that is written a lot and rarely read.

challenges.title: Counting likes
challenges.brief:
A short-video app records every like as a database row update. During a viral dance trend, the counter rows for a few videos are locked thousands of times a second and the whole database slows down.

Counts may be a few seconds behind, but the app must absorb the flood.
functional: Like and unlike videos
Show like counts on every video
nonFunctional: Absorb millions of likes per minute
Counts may lag a few seconds; they must not drift permanently

estimate.q: How many likes per second at peak?
estimate.workings: 3,000,000 / 60 s = 50,000 likes per second. Batched every 10 s, that becomes one update per video per flush.

tradeoff.q: What is the risk of write-behind?
choices: Counts are always wrong.
Likes still waiting in the cache are lost if the cache fails before the next flush.
Reads become slower than the database.
tradeoff.why: Write-behind acknowledges writes from memory. Replicating the cache and flushing often shrinks the window, but it never fully closes — fine for likes, wrong for payments.

challenges.learn:
**Write-behind** turns thousands of tiny writes into one batch: counters grow in the cache and a worker flushes the totals to the database every few seconds.

The trade-off is durability — anything not yet flushed can be lost. Use it where losing a few seconds of data is acceptable.

challenges.title: Stampede
challenges.brief:
A celebrity posts on a social site. Their post is cached with a 60-second TTL and read 20,000 times a second. Every minute, when the key expires, thousands of requests miss at the same instant, all run the same 200 ms query, and the database falls over.

Keep the cache, but stop the herd.
functional: Show the celebrity's post to everyone
Refresh the cached post every minute
nonFunctional: A key expiring never sends a burst of identical queries to the database

numbers.label: Reads of the hot key per second

estimate.q: Without protection, about how many requests miss during the 200 ms rebuild?
estimate.workings: 20,000 req/s × 0.2 s = 4,000 requests, each sending the same query to the database.

tradeoff.q: Which technique stops a stampede?
choices: Lowering the TTL to one second.
Letting a single request rebuild the value (a lock or "single flight") while the rest wait briefly or get the stale value.
Adding more database indexes.
tradeoff.why: The fix is coordination: one rebuild per key. Serving the slightly stale value while it refreshes keeps latency flat, at the cost of a few extra milliseconds of staleness.

challenges.learn:
A **cache stampede** turns one expiry into thousands of identical database queries. **Stampede protection** (a per-key lock, request coalescing, or early refresh) makes sure only one request rebuilds the value.

The trade-off is serving slightly stale data or making a few requests wait — much cheaper than an outage.

challenges.title: Ghost keys
challenges.brief:
A second-hand marketplace exposes `GET /items/{id}`. Scraper bots request millions of random IDs that don't exist. Every one misses the cache (there is nothing to cache) and reaches the database.

Stop lookups for non-existent items before they reach the database, without slowing down real ones.
functional: Look up items by ID
Answer "not found" quickly for IDs that don't exist
nonFunctional: Requests for missing IDs don't reach the database
Real lookups stay fast

estimate.q: A Bloom filter needs about 9.6 bits per item for a 1% false-positive rate. How big is the filter for all items?
estimate.workings: 100M × 9.6 bits = 960M bits ÷ 8 = 120,000,000 bytes ≈ 120 MB — it fits in memory easily.

tradeoff.q: A Bloom filter says "maybe present" for an ID. What happens next?
choices: The item definitely exists; return it without looking.
Check the cache and database as usual; about 1% of lookups for missing IDs slip through as false "maybe" answers and are caught there.
Reject the request.
tradeoff.why: Bloom filters have no false negatives but some false positives. "No" is trusted; "maybe" is checked. You trade a little memory and a rebuild process for skipping almost all ghost lookups.

challenges.learn:
A **Bloom filter** answers "definitely not here" from memory, so lookups for missing keys never reach the database. **Negative caching** (storing "not found" briefly) is a simpler alternative when the same missing keys repeat.

The trade-off: the filter must be kept up to date as items are added, and deletions need a periodic rebuild.

challenges.title: Avalanche
challenges.brief:
A travel site warms its cache at 3 a.m. by loading a million hotel pages, all with a one-hour TTL. At 4 a.m. every key expires in the same second, the database takes the full load at once, and the site goes down for ten minutes. It happens again after each deploy.

Spread the expiries out and make the cache itself less fragile.
functional: Show hotel pages from cache
Refresh hotel data about hourly
nonFunctional: Keys never all expire at once
Losing one cache node doesn't send all traffic to the database

estimate.q: With ±10% jitter on a 1-hour TTL, expiries spread over 12 minutes. About how many keys expire per second?
estimate.workings: ±10% of 60 min = a 12-minute window = 720 s; 1,000,000 / 720 ≈ 1,389 per second instead of 1M in one second.

tradeoff.q: Why does adding random jitter to TTLs help?
choices: It makes every key live longer.
Keys loaded together expire at slightly different times, so refreshes arrive as a steady trickle instead of one flood.
It encrypts the cache.
tradeoff.why: Jitter trades exact TTLs for a smooth refresh rate. Nobody cares whether a hotel page refreshes after 57 or 63 minutes; the database cares a lot.

challenges.learn:
A **cache avalanche** happens when many keys share an expiry time or a cache node dies. **TTL jitter** spreads expiries; **several cache replicas** mean one failure doesn't dump everything on the database.

The trade-off is slightly less predictable freshness and the cost of extra cache nodes.

challenges.title: Cache the API
challenges.brief:
A hardware store publishes a public product API that price-comparison sites poll constantly: `GET /products/123`, the same answers again and again. The app servers spend 80% of their time rebuilding identical JSON.

Cache whole responses before they reach the app. Prices change a few times a day; a minute of staleness is fine.
functional: Serve public product endpoints
Price changes show up within a minute
nonFunctional: Repeated identical requests don't reach the app servers

estimate.q: With an 80% hit ratio, how many requests per second still reach the app servers?

tradeoff.q: Which requests must never be served from a shared response cache?
choices: Public product pages.
Responses that depend on who is asking, like a logged-in user's basket, unless the cache key includes the user.
Images.
tradeoff.why: A shared cache returns one copy to everyone who asks the same URL. Personalised responses must be marked private or not cached at all, or users will see each other's data.

challenges.learn:
**HTTP response caching** at a reverse proxy or CDN answers repeated GETs without running any app code. Either place works; a CDN is also close to users.

The trade-off is staleness bounded by the TTL, and the discipline to never cache personalised responses in a shared cache.

challenges.title: Who gets evicted?
challenges.brief:
A recipe app caches recipes in a small 2 GB cache. A few hundred classics (pancakes, lasagne) are read all day. Every night a crawler reads through the whole archive once — and by morning the classics have been pushed out of the cache and the database is swamped.

Choose an eviction policy that keeps the always-popular items.
functional: Serve recipes from cache when possible
nonFunctional: One-off scans don't evict the always-popular recipes
The cache stays at 2 GB

estimate.q: At 4 KB per recipe, how many recipes fit in a 2 GB cache?
estimate.workings: 2,000,000 KB / 4 KB = 500,000 recipes — a quarter of the archive, so the nightly scan fills it several times over.

tradeoff.q: When is LRU a better choice than LFU?
choices: Never.
When popularity shifts quickly (today's news), because LFU keeps yesterday's favourites that have built up high counts.
When the cache is very large.
tradeoff.why: LRU favours what was used recently; LFU favours what is used often. LFU resists one-off scans but adapts slowly to new trends, so it usually counts with ageing.

challenges.learn:
**Eviction** decides what a full cache forgets. **LRU** drops the least recently used item, so one long scan can flush it. **LFU** drops the least frequently used, protecting steady favourites.

The trade-off: LFU adapts more slowly when popularity shifts.

challenges.title: Breaking news
challenges.brief:
A national news site normally serves 2,000 requests a second. When big news breaks, traffic jumps 50× within five minutes — far too fast for new servers to boot — and everyone reads the same handful of articles.

Layer caches so the spike never reaches the database, and do it within the monthly budget: buying 50× the servers is not an option.
functional: Readers load articles and the home page
Editors publish updates every few minutes
nonFunctional: Survive 50× traffic with no warning
Updates visible within a minute
Stay within budget

numbers.label: CDN hit ratio in a spike

estimate.q: During the spike, how many requests per second get past the CDN?
estimate.workings: 2,000 × 50 = 100,000 req/s; 5% misses = 5,000 req/s reach the origin, and the proxy cache absorbs most of those.

tradeoff.q: Why layer several caches instead of one big one?
choices: Each layer is cheaper than the next and catches most of what the previous one missed, so very little reaches the expensive tiers.
One cache can't hold text.
More layers always make data fresher.
tradeoff.why: The CDN absorbs the flood near readers, the proxy cache catches most misses, and the app cache protects the database. The cost is that staleness can add up across layers, so TTLs must be short and deliberate.

challenges.learn:
Traffic spikes are survived with **layers of caching**: CDN at the edge, a proxy cache in front of the app, an app cache in front of the database, and **read replicas** behind that. Each layer shrinks the load on the next.

The trade-off is freshness: every layer can serve a slightly older copy, so short TTLs and stampede protection matter.

challenges.title: Two is one
challenges.brief:
A booking tool for hair salons runs on a single app server. Last Tuesday it crashed during the lunch rush and 3,000 salons couldn't take appointments for 40 minutes.

"Two is one and one is none." Make sure one server crashing is invisible to users.
functional: Salons view and book appointments
nonFunctional: A single server crash causes no outage
Broken servers stop receiving traffic automatically

estimate.q: If one server handles 500 req/s, how many servers do you need so the 400 req/s peak survives one failure?
estimate.workings: One server covers the peak, so N + 1 = 2 servers: if either dies, the other still handles 400 req/s.

tradeoff.q: Why put the two app servers in different availability zones?
choices: Zones are cheaper.
A power or network failure in one data centre then takes out only one server.
Servers in the same zone can't talk to each other.
tradeoff.why: Two servers on the same rack can fail together. Spreading them across zones costs a little cross-zone traffic and survives a whole data centre going dark.

challenges.learn:
Redundancy needs three things: **at least two servers**, a **load balancer** in front, and **health checks** so traffic stops going to the broken one.

Placing copies in different **availability zones** protects against failures bigger than one machine. The cost is paying for capacity you hope never to need.

challenges.title: Route by path
challenges.brief:
An e-learning site serves its API (`/api/…`) and its course videos' thumbnails and pages (`/static/…`) from the same servers. A popular course launch floods `/static` and the API slows to a crawl.

Send each kind of path to its own fleet, behind one public address.

`/static/*` goes to the static fleet
nonFunctional: A flood on one path doesn't slow the other
One public address for both

tradeoff.q: Why does path-based routing need an L7 load balancer?
choices: L4 balancers are slower at everything.
An L4 balancer sees only IP addresses and ports; it must read the HTTP request to see the path, which is layer 7.
L7 balancers are the only ones with health checks.
tradeoff.why: L7 parses each request, so it can route by path, host or header and terminate TLS. The cost is more CPU per request than L4, which just forwards connections.

challenges.learn:
An **L7** load balancer reads HTTP, so it can send `/api` and `/static` to different fleets and scale each one separately.

The trade-off: L7 does more work per request than **L4**, which only forwards connections and can't see paths.

challenges.title: Unstick
challenges.brief:
A fitness app turned on sticky sessions years ago because its servers kept workouts-in-progress in memory. Now one server regularly runs at 95% CPU while others idle, and deploys log people out mid-workout.

The current design is on the canvas. Make the servers interchangeable again.
functional: Members track workouts in progress
Any server can continue any member's workout
nonFunctional: Load spreads evenly
Deploying or losing a server doesn't lose workouts in progress

estimate.q: Three servers at 95%, 20% and 25% CPU. What would each run at if the load were spread evenly?

tradeoff.q: Why does stickiness make load uneven?
choices: It doesn't; stickiness balances perfectly.
Users are pinned when they start, so a few heavy users or a burst of new logins can pile onto one server that can't shed them.
Sticky balancers ignore health checks.
tradeoff.why: Stickiness lets the balancer decide only once per user. Without it, every request can go to the least-loaded server — once the servers keep no state.

challenges.learn:
Sticky sessions are a crutch for **stateful** servers. Move the state into a **shared store**, turn stickiness off, and the balancer can send each request to whichever server is least busy.

The trade-off is a store round-trip per request — small compared with an overloaded server.

challenges.title: Flash sale
challenges.brief:
A sneaker shop runs a sale every Friday at noon. Traffic climbs from 1,500 to 15,000 requests a second over about twenty minutes, stays there for an hour, then falls back. Paying for peak capacity all week is wasteful.

Let the app tier grow and shrink by itself, with a safe floor and a cost ceiling.
functional: Shoppers browse and buy during the sale
nonFunctional: Handle 10× normal traffic
Don't pay for peak capacity all week
Never drop below a safe minimum

estimate.q: How many app servers are needed at the peak?
estimate.workings: 15,000 / 500 = 30 servers, versus 3 the rest of the week.

tradeoff.q: Why does autoscaling alone not save you from a sudden 10× spike in one minute?
choices: Autoscaling only works at night.
New servers take minutes to boot and warm up, so the spike arrives before they do. Scale ahead of known events or add caching and queues.
Autoscaling can only add one server per day.
tradeoff.why: Autoscaling follows trends. For scheduled peaks, raise the minimum before noon; for sudden ones, rely on caches and backpressure.

challenges.learn:
**Autoscaling** adds and removes servers between a **minimum** (safety) and a **maximum** (cost). It only works if servers are **stateless**, so new ones can join instantly.

The trade-off is lag: servers take minutes to start, so planned peaks need a raised floor ahead of time.

challenges.title: Stop the scrapers
challenges.brief:
A weather API gives each customer 100 requests a minute. A few free-tier accounts run scrapers that send thousands, and paying customers see timeouts. The API runs behind several gateway instances, so a limit counted in one gateway's memory lets a client get 100 per instance.

Enforce each customer's limit across all instances.
functional: Customers call the weather API with a key
Customers over their limit get a clear "429 Too Many Requests"
nonFunctional: A client's limit holds no matter which gateway instance serves it
The limit check adds under 2 ms

estimate.q: If each of 4 gateway instances counted separately, how many requests per minute could one client really make?
estimate.workings: 100 per instance × 4 instances = 400 per minute — four times the limit.

tradeoff.q: What is the cost of keeping counters in a shared store?
choices: None.
An extra network call on every request, and the store becomes something the API depends on — decide whether to allow or block traffic if it is down.
Counters become less accurate.
tradeoff.why: Shared counters are accurate across instances but add latency and a dependency. Most teams "fail open" (allow traffic) if the counter store is unreachable.

challenges.learn:
**Rate limiting** protects everyone from a few heavy clients. With several gateway instances, counters must live in a **shared, fast store** (usually a cache), or each instance grants its own quota.

The trade-off is an extra sub-millisecond call per request and a decision about what to do if the store is down.

challenges.title: Around the world
challenges.brief:
A language-learning app is hosted in Europe. Half its users are in South America, where every tap takes 250 ms before anything happens. Lessons are read far more than progress is written.

Serve each continent from its own region, with a load balancer and app servers in each, and send users to the nearest one.

Users are served from the nearest region
nonFunctional: Lesson loads under 100 ms on both continents
Either region can keep serving if the other has problems

estimate.q: A lesson screen makes 5 sequential requests. How much waiting does a 200 ms round trip add compared with ~20 ms locally?
estimate.workings: 5 × 200 ms = 1,000 ms versus 5 × 20 ms = 100 ms: about 900 ms more per screen.

tradeoff.q: Where should progress writes go when the primary database is in Europe?
choices: To the local read replica, which forwards nothing.
To the European primary — slower for South American users, but writes stay consistent; reads stay local via the replica.
Nowhere; progress is only stored on the phone.
tradeoff.why: With one primary, remote writes pay the long round trip while reads are fast. Accepting multi-region writes needs conflict handling — a later chapter.

challenges.learn:
**Geo DNS** sends each user to the nearest region, where a local **load balancer** and app servers answer. Local **read replicas** make reads fast everywhere.

The trade-off: with a single primary, writes from the far region still cross the ocean, and replicas there may lag a little.
