challenges.title: Hot partition
challenges.brief:
A social app shards posts by author across eight databases. It worked beautifully until a pop star joined: now one shard takes 70% of all reads, and adding shards changes nothing because every read of her posts still lands on the same one.

Keep the sharding, but stop one key from melting its shard.
functional: Read posts by author
Most reads target a handful of famous authors
nonFunctional: No single shard is overloaded by one key
Normal authors are unaffected

estimate.q: 1M fans refresh her page once a minute. How many reads per second hit her shard?
estimate.workings: 1,000,000 / 60 s ≈ 16,700 reads/s — more than three times what one shard can serve.

tradeoff.q: Why doesn't adding more shards fix a hot key?
choices: Shards can't be added.
A key always maps to exactly one shard, so its traffic moves with it; you have to cache it or split the key itself.
More shards make hashing slower.
tradeoff.why: Sharding spreads different keys, not one key. Caching absorbs reads of hot keys; for hot writes, you split the key (e.g. add a random suffix and merge on read).

challenges.learn:
A **hot partition** is a key too popular for any one shard. Put a **cache** in front of the shards (with replicas, so the cache doesn't become the new hotspot) or split the key with a salted suffix.

The trade-off: cached reads may be slightly stale, and salted keys make reads fan out.

rules.text: Posts are sharded through a router
rules.hint: Keep the sharding.

rules.text: The router has at least three shards
rules.hint: Draw the shards.

rules.text: Hot posts are served from a cache before the shards
rules.hint: What absorbs 16,700 reads a second of the same key?

rules.text: The cache itself isn't a single hot node
rules.hint: Give the cache several replicas so reads of the hot key spread out.

rules.text: Shards use consistent hashing
rules.hint: Adding a shard should move few keys.

rules.text: The hot key expiring doesn't cause a herd
rules.hint: Everyone reads it at once.

challenges.title: Backpressure
challenges.brief:
A photo-printing service accepts uploads faster than its workers can prepare them for print. The job queue has no limit: it grows all afternoon, memory runs out at 5 p.m., and every job is lost.

When the system is full, it should say "try again in a minute" at the door instead of collapsing later.
functional: Customers upload print jobs
Workers prepare jobs for printing
nonFunctional: The system never runs out of memory from backlog
Excess requests are rejected early and clearly

estimate.q: How much does the backlog grow per hour at peak?
estimate.workings: (1,200 − 800) jobs/min × 60 min = 24,000 jobs per hour.

tradeoff.q: Why reject some requests instead of queueing them all?
choices: Rejecting is always rude, so never do it.
An unbounded queue only delays the failure and makes every job slow; a fast, clear rejection keeps the system healthy for the jobs it accepts.
Queues can't hold more than ten jobs.
tradeoff.why: Backpressure admits only what can be finished in reasonable time. Some customers retry later, but nobody's job is lost in a crash.

challenges.learn:
**Backpressure** means a full system pushes back: the queue has a **maximum size**, and the front door **sheds load** (HTTP 429/503) when it is reached.

The trade-off is turning some customers away at peak — honest and recoverable, unlike a crash that loses everything.

rules.text: Uploads come in through a gateway
rules.hint: Something at the door must be able to say "not now".

rules.text: The gateway sheds load when the system is full
rules.hint: Look at the gateway's properties.

rules.text: Jobs wait in a queue for workers
rules.hint: Put a queue between accepting a job and doing it.

rules.text: The queue has a maximum size
rules.hint: An unbounded queue grows until memory runs out.

rules.text: Several workers drain the queue
rules.hint: More than one worker.

rules.text: Jobs that keep failing are parked
rules.hint: A broken job shouldn't be retried forever.

challenges.title: A million sockets
challenges.brief:
A live sports app pushes score updates to fans the instant they happen. At a final, a million fans hold WebSocket connections open for two hours. One gateway can hold about 100,000 connections.

Fans connected to different gateways must all get every update.
functional: Fans keep a live connection open
Every fan receives every score update within a second
nonFunctional: Hold 1M concurrent connections
Losing one gateway disconnects only its fans, who reconnect elsewhere

estimate.q: How many WebSocket gateways do you need for the final?
estimate.workings: 1,000,000 / 100,000 = 10 gateways, plus spare capacity for a failure.

tradeoff.q: Why use an L4 load balancer in front of WebSocket gateways?
choices: L4 balancers can read WebSocket messages.
Connections last hours; L4 simply forwards each TCP connection to a gateway cheaply, without parsing every frame.
L7 balancers can't forward traffic.
tradeoff.why: For long-lived connections the balancer's job is to pick a gateway once. L4 does that with little overhead; L7 is needed only if you route by URL or headers.

challenges.learn:
Push at scale needs many **WebSocket gateways** behind an **L4** load balancer, and a **pub/sub** channel so an update published once reaches every gateway — and through them every fan.

The trade-off: each gateway holds lots of memory per connection, and a gateway failure means reconnect storms that clients must back off from.

rules.text: Connections arrive through an L4 load balancer
rules.hint: Long-lived connections need only to be forwarded.

rules.text: At least three WebSocket gateways
rules.hint: One gateway can't hold them all, and one failure shouldn't drop everyone.

rules.text: Updates reach every gateway through pub/sub
rules.hint: Every gateway subscribes to one topic; draw the topic → gateway delivery.

rules.text: Score updates are published by the scores service
rules.hint: Who publishes the update in the first place?

rules.text: Enough gateways for a million fans
rules.hint: Use your estimate.

rules.text: Broken gateways get no new connections
rules.hint: Health checks.

challenges.title: Ticket rush
challenges.brief:
A stadium tour goes on sale at 10:00. 500,000 fans are waiting for 20,000 seats. Last time, the site crashed in 30 seconds, then sold some seats twice when it came back.

Design a fair, stable sale: let fans in at a pace the system can handle, keep bots in check, grow the app tier for the rush, and never sell a seat twice.
functional: Fans join the sale and wait their turn
Fans pick seats and pay
Each seat is sold once
nonFunctional: Survives 500,000 simultaneous fans
No seat is ever sold twice
Bots can't grab all the tickets

estimate.q: If fans are let in at the rate the database can handle, how long until every seat is sold?
estimate.workings: 20,000 seats / 500 purchases per second = 40 seconds of selling; everyone else waits in the queue meanwhile.

tradeoff.q: Why a waiting room instead of letting everyone hit "buy" at once?
choices: Queues make the tickets cheaper.
It turns an impossible spike into a steady flow the database can handle, and gives fans a fair, first-come order instead of a crash.
The waiting room removes the need for locking.
tradeoff.why: The queue caps concurrency at what the checkout can do. It doesn't remove races between the fans who are let in — locking still guarantees one buyer per seat.

challenges.learn:
A sale spike is tamed in layers: a **rate limit** at the gateway, a **waiting-room queue** that admits fans at the pace checkout can handle, an **autoscaling** app tier, and **locking** in the database so each seat is sold once.

The trade-off is waiting: fans queue for minutes instead of racing — but the sale finishes and nobody gets a double-sold seat.

rules.text: Fans arrive through a rate-limited gateway
rules.hint: Slow down bots at the door.

rules.text: Purchases wait in a queue and are processed at a steady pace
rules.hint: A waiting room is a queue in front of checkout.

rules.text: The app tier autoscales
rules.hint: The rush starts at a known time.

rules.text: A seat can only be sold once
rules.hint: Look at the database's locking option.

rules.text: Fans pay through a payment provider
rules.hint: Who charges the card?

rules.text: The waiting room has a size limit
rules.hint: Even a queue can overflow.

rules.text: The seat map is cached
rules.hint: Everyone reads the same seat map.

rules.text: Static pages come from a CDN
rules.hint: The waiting-room page itself can be served from the edge.

rules.text: Clients don't talk to the database directly
rules.hint: Keep storage behind your servers.

challenges.title: Don't make them wait
challenges.brief:
A meal-kit company's signup page takes four seconds because the server sends the welcome email before answering. When the email provider has a bad day, signups fail altogether.

Answer the new customer right away and send the email in the background.
functional: Customers sign up
A welcome email is sent after signup
nonFunctional: Signup responds in under 300 ms
Signup works even when the email provider is down

estimate.q: If each signup waits 800 ms for the email call, how many signups are waiting at once at peak?
estimate.workings: 50 signups/s × 0.8 s = 40 requests tied up just waiting on email.

tradeoff.q: What does the customer lose when the email is sent in the background?
choices: Only immediacy — the email goes out a few seconds later instead of during the request, and signup no longer depends on the provider being up.
They never get the email.
Their account isn't saved.
tradeoff.why: The trade-off is that the page can't promise the email has been sent — only that it will be. If the provider is down, the queue holds the job until it recovers.

challenges.learn:
Move slow, non-essential work out of the request: the app saves the signup, drops a job in a **queue** and answers. A **worker** sends the email when it can.

The trade-off is **eventual** completion: the email may arrive seconds (or, during an outage, hours) later, and you now run a queue and workers.

rules.text: Signups are saved by the app
rules.hint: The account itself must be saved before answering.

rules.text: The app hands the email job to a queue
rules.hint: Put a queue between the app and the slow work.

rules.text: A worker sends the email
rules.hint: The worker talks to the email provider.

rules.text: Emails that keep failing are parked
rules.hint: Set retries on the queue and give it a dead-letter queue.

rules.text: A retried job doesn't send two emails
rules.hint: Look at the worker's properties.

rules.text: The app doesn't call the email provider during signup
rules.hint: A direct call brings the four-second wait back.

challenges.title: Tell everyone
challenges.brief:
When an order is placed at a furniture shop, the customer gets an email and an SMS, and the analytics team records the sale. The order service calls all three itself, and every new team that wants to react to orders asks the order team for another change.

Publish the event once and let anyone subscribe.
functional: Orders trigger an email, an SMS and an analytics record
New consumers can be added without changing the order service
nonFunctional: One slow consumer doesn't delay the others or the order

estimate.q: With 3 consumers, how many messages are delivered per day?
estimate.workings: 40,000 orders × 3 subscribers = 120,000 deliveries; the order service still publishes only 40,000.

tradeoff.q: What is harder with publish/subscribe than with direct calls?
choices: Adding new consumers.
Seeing the whole flow: the publisher doesn't know who reacts, so tracing and handling a failed consumer take deliberate effort.
Sending messages to more than one place.
tradeoff.why: Pub/sub removes coupling, and with it the single place that shows everything an order triggers. Good naming, tracing and per-consumer monitoring make up for it.

challenges.learn:
With **pub/sub** the order service publishes "order placed" once; every subscriber gets its own copy. Adding a consumer never touches the publisher.

The trade-off: the flow is spread out and harder to see, and each subscriber must handle its own failures and retries.

rules.text: Orders are published to a topic
rules.hint: The order service publishes once.

rules.text: At least three subscribers receive each order
rules.hint: Draw one subscriber per reaction.

rules.text: A subscriber sends the email
rules.hint: Follow the topic to the email provider.

rules.text: A subscriber sends the SMS
rules.hint: Follow the topic to the SMS provider.

rules.text: A subscriber records the sale for analytics
rules.hint: Where does the analytics team keep sales?

rules.text: Subscribers buffer in their own queues
rules.hint: A queue per subscriber lets each one fall behind safely.

rules.text: The order service doesn't call the providers itself
rules.hint: Direct calls re-couple the order service to every consumer.

challenges.title: Poison pill
challenges.brief:
An invoicing service processes invoices from a queue. Yesterday one invoice with a malformed date crashed the worker, went back to the queue, crashed the next worker, and so on for six hours. Thousands of good invoices waited behind it.

Make sure one bad message can't block the queue.
functional: Workers turn orders into invoices
Broken messages are set aside for a human to inspect
nonFunctional: One bad message never blocks the rest
No message is silently lost

estimate.q: At a 0.01% failure rate, how many invoices a day end up in the dead-letter queue?
estimate.workings: 5,000 × 24 = 120,000 invoices × 0.0001 = 12 per day — few enough for a human to inspect.

tradeoff.q: Why not just drop a message after it fails five times?
choices: Dropping is fine; bad messages are worthless.
Each one is a real invoice; parking it in a dead-letter queue keeps it for inspection, fixing and replay, and gives you an alert signal.
Queues can't drop messages.
tradeoff.why: A DLQ trades a bit of storage and an on-call chore for never silently losing work. An alert on its size tells you when something systematic breaks.

challenges.learn:
Limit **retries** and send messages that keep failing to a **dead-letter queue**. The main queue keeps flowing, and nothing is lost: someone fixes the cause and replays the parked messages.

The trade-off is operational: a DLQ needs monitoring, or it becomes a silent graveyard.

rules.text: Invoices are processed from a queue by workers
rules.hint: Keep the queue and workers.

rules.text: Each message is retried a limited number of times
rules.hint: Look at the queue's retry setting.

rules.text: Messages that keep failing go to a dead-letter queue
rules.hint: Where do they go after the last retry?

rules.text: Invoices are saved
rules.hint: The worker's output needs a home.

rules.text: Someone is alerted when messages pile up in the DLQ
rules.hint: A DLQ nobody watches is a graveyard.

rules.text: Retried invoices aren't created twice
rules.hint: Look at the worker's properties.

challenges.title: Competing consumers
challenges.brief:
A document-scanning service turns uploaded PDFs into searchable text. One worker handles 150 pages a minute, but 450 arrive every minute during office hours. The backlog grows all day and customers wait until the next morning.

Let more workers share the same queue.
functional: Uploaded pages are turned into text
nonFunctional: The backlog doesn't grow during office hours
A worker crash doesn't lose pages

estimate.q: How many workers keep up with the arrivals?
estimate.workings: 450 / 150 = 3 workers just to keep pace; a 4th gives room to catch up after a spike.

tradeoff.q: What do you give up when several workers consume one queue?
choices: Nothing at all.
Strict ordering: two workers process messages in parallel, so page 2 may finish before page 1.
Messages are delivered to every worker.
tradeoff.why: Competing consumers scale throughput by processing in parallel. If order matters (it doesn't for independent pages), use partitions instead.

challenges.learn:
**Competing consumers**: several workers read from one queue and each message goes to one of them. Throughput grows roughly linearly with workers.

The trade-off is ordering: messages finish in whatever order the workers happen to finish them.

rules.text: Uploads are stored and queued
rules.hint: Pages are saved, then a job is queued.

rules.text: Workers take jobs from the queue
rules.hint: Connect the queue to the workers.

rules.text: At least three workers share the queue
rules.hint: Use your estimate.

rules.text: Extracted text is saved
rules.hint: Where does the text go?

rules.text: A spare worker to catch up after spikes
rules.hint: Keeping pace isn't catching up.

rules.text: Unreadable pages don't block the queue
rules.hint: Retries and a dead-letter queue.

challenges.title: Order matters
challenges.brief:
A bank sends account events — "deposit 100", "withdraw 80" — to a queue with several workers. Sometimes the withdrawal is processed first, the balance goes negative for a moment, and an overdraft fee is charged wrongly.

Keep each account's events in order, while different accounts are still processed in parallel.
functional: Apply account events to balances
Several workers share the work
nonFunctional: Events of one account are applied in the order they happened
Throughput grows with more workers

estimate.q: With 12 partitions and 6 workers in one consumer group, how many partitions does each worker read?
estimate.workings: 12 / 6 = 2 partitions per worker. More partitions than workers leaves room to add workers later.

tradeoff.q: Why partition by account ID instead of using a single partition?
choices: A single partition keeps global order but only one worker can read it, so throughput stops growing.
Single partitions lose messages.
Account IDs are random, so order doesn't matter.
tradeoff.why: Order is needed per account, not globally. Partitioning by account ID keeps each account in one ordered partition while spreading accounts across many.

challenges.learn:
An **event stream** keeps order **within a partition**. Using the account ID as **partition key** puts all of an account's events in one partition, and a **consumer group** spreads partitions across workers.

The trade-off: parallelism is capped at the number of partitions, and one very busy account can't be split.

rules.text: Events flow through an event stream
rules.hint: A plain queue with competing workers can reorder events.

rules.text: Events are partitioned by account
rules.hint: Fill in the stream's partition key.

rules.text: The stream has several partitions
rules.hint: One partition means one worker.

rules.text: Workers share the stream as a consumer group
rules.hint: Look at the stream's consumer group option.

rules.text: Balances are stored
rules.hint: The workers update balances somewhere durable.

rules.text: Several workers share the partitions
rules.hint: Scale the workers.

rules.text: A plain queue with several workers can reorder events
rules.hint: Competing consumers process in parallel with no per-key order.

challenges.title: Remind me later
challenges.brief:
A dental clinic network books appointments weeks ahead. Patients should get a reminder 24 hours before. Today a script runs every minute, scans every future appointment and times out as the table grows.

Schedule each reminder when the appointment is booked, and send it at the right time.
functional: Patients book appointments
Each patient gets a reminder 24 hours before
nonFunctional: Reminders go out within a minute of the right time
Nothing scans the whole appointments table

estimate.q: How many future appointments exist at any time (8-week horizon)?
estimate.workings: 20,000 per day × 56 days = 1,120,000 rows the old script scanned every minute.

tradeoff.q: What must the reminder worker check before sending?
choices: Nothing; the message says everything.
That the appointment still exists at that time — it may have been cancelled or moved after the reminder was scheduled.
That the queue is empty.
tradeoff.why: A delayed message is a snapshot of the past. Re-reading the current state before acting avoids reminding people of cancelled appointments.

challenges.learn:
**Delayed delivery** lets you enqueue a message now that becomes visible later — exactly "remind in N hours", with no table scans. A scheduler that picks due items from an indexed table works too.

The trade-off: delayed messages can go stale, so the worker re-checks the appointment before sending.

rules.text: Patients book through the app
rules.hint: Appointments are saved when booked.

rules.text: Each reminder is scheduled to fire later
rules.hint: Either a queue with delayed delivery, or a scheduler starting the reminder worker.

rules.text: A worker sends the reminder
rules.hint: Push or SMS.

rules.text: The worker re-checks the appointment before sending
rules.hint: It may have been cancelled.

rules.text: A retried reminder isn't sent twice
rules.hint: Look at the worker's properties.

challenges.title: Replay the past
challenges.brief:
A music app streams "song played" events that the billing service uses to pay artists. Now a new recommendations service needs the last 30 days of plays to learn listeners' tastes — but the stream keeps only 7 days.

The current design is on the canvas. Let the new service replay a month of history without disturbing billing.
functional: Billing keeps consuming plays as today
Recommendations reads the last 30 days of plays, then keeps up
nonFunctional: The new consumer doesn't slow down or affect billing
No change to the app that produces the events

estimate.q: How much data does the stream hold with 30 days of retention?
estimate.workings: 200M × 200 bytes = 40 GB per day; × 30 days = 1,200 GB ≈ 1.2 TB.

tradeoff.q: Why doesn't the new service's replay affect billing?
choices: Because the stream deletes events after billing reads them.
Each consumer group keeps its own position in the log, so recommendations can read from 30 days ago while billing stays at the latest event.
Because recommendations uses a different stream.
tradeoff.why: Streams are logs, not queues: reading doesn't remove events. The cost is storing more history — 1.2 TB here — for as long as someone might need to replay it.

challenges.learn:
An **event stream** keeps events for its **retention** period and lets each **consumer group** read at its own pace. A new service can start from the beginning and rebuild its data from history.

The trade-off is storage: longer retention costs more disk, so size it for the longest replay you actually need.

rules.text: The stream keeps at least 30 days of events
rules.hint: Look at the stream's retention.

rules.text: Billing still consumes the stream
rules.hint: Don't break billing.

rules.text: Recommendations consumes the same stream
rules.hint: Add the new service as another consumer.

rules.text: Consumers read independently
rules.hint: Each service should keep its own position.

rules.text: Recommendations keeps its own data
rules.hint: Don't reach into billing's database.

challenges.title: Exactly once-ish
challenges.brief:
A subscription box company charges customers monthly from a queue of "charge" messages. When a worker crashes after charging but before acknowledging, the message is delivered again — and the customer is charged twice.

You can't make the network deliver exactly once. Make processing behave as if it did.
functional: Charge each subscriber once per month
nonFunctional: No charge message is lost
No subscriber is charged twice for the same month

estimate.q: At a 0.1% redelivery rate, how many double charges per month would happen without deduplication?
estimate.workings: 2,000,000 × 0.001 = 2,000 angry customers a month.

tradeoff.q: Why choose at-least-once delivery and deduplicate, rather than at-most-once?
choices: At-most-once is slower.
At-most-once can silently lose a charge; at-least-once never loses one, and deduplication removes the repeats.
At-least-once needs no worker changes.
tradeoff.why: You pick which failure you prefer. Losing money silently is worse than handling duplicates, which idempotency keys and a dedup store make harmless.

challenges.learn:
"Exactly once" in practice is **at-least-once delivery** plus **idempotent processing**: every message carries an ID (subscriber + month), the worker checks a **dedup store** before acting, passes the ID to the provider as an idempotency key, and records it once the charge succeeds. (Recording it *before* charging would turn a crash into a lost charge.)

The trade-off is an extra lookup per message and keeping those IDs long enough to catch late redeliveries.

rules.text: Charges are processed from a queue
rules.hint: Keep the queue and workers.

rules.text: No charge message is ever lost
rules.hint: Look at the queue's delivery guarantee.

rules.text: Workers process charges idempotently
rules.hint: Look at the worker's properties.

rules.text: Workers record which charges were already made
rules.hint: Where can a worker check "did I already charge this subscriber this month"?

rules.text: Workers charge through the payment provider
rules.hint: Who moves the money?

rules.text: The provider call carries an idempotency key and retries safely
rules.hint: Retry the provider call with backoff; the key makes repeats harmless on their side too.

challenges.title: Video pipeline
challenges.brief:
A cooking school lets instructors upload lesson videos. Students watch on phones, tablets and TVs, so every video is needed in 360p, 720p, 1080p and 4K. Transcoding a 20-minute video takes about 10 minutes of CPU per resolution.

Build the pipeline from upload to playback.
functional: Instructors upload videos
Each video is transcoded into four resolutions
Students stream the right resolution
nonFunctional: Uploads don't pass through app servers
A failed transcode is retried, not lost
Playback is smooth worldwide

estimate.q: How many transcoders must run in parallel to keep up with a day's uploads?
estimate.workings: 2,000 × 4 × 10 min = 80,000 CPU-minutes per day; a day has 1,440 minutes; 80,000 / 1,440 ≈ 56 transcoders busy all day.

tradeoff.q: Why put a queue between upload and transcoding?
choices: Queues make videos smaller.
Uploads arrive in bursts; the queue holds jobs until a transcoder is free, retries failures, and lets you scale transcoders independently.
Transcoders can't read from storage directly.
tradeoff.why: The queue decouples fast, bursty uploads from slow, expensive transcoding. The cost is latency: a video may wait a while before it is ready to watch.

challenges.learn:
A **media pipeline**: upload straight to storage, an event puts a job on a **queue**, **transcoders** produce each resolution back into storage, and a **CDN** serves them.

The trade-off is time-to-publish: videos appear minutes after upload, and transcoding capacity is the most expensive part to size.

rules.text: Videos are uploaded straight to object storage
rules.hint: The bytes should skip the app servers.

rules.text: Each upload creates a transcoding job in a queue
rules.hint: Something must tell the transcoders there is work.

rules.text: Transcoded files go back to object storage
rules.hint: Where do the renditions live?

rules.text: Students watch through a CDN
rules.hint: Video is heavy; serve it from the edge.

rules.text: Several transcoders share the work
rules.hint: One transcoder can't keep up.

rules.text: Uploads use signed URLs
rules.hint: Instructors shouldn't get storage credentials.

rules.text: Failed transcodes are retried, then parked
rules.hint: Retries and a dead-letter queue.

challenges.title: Notification system
challenges.brief:
A company with dozens of internal services wants one notification platform. Services call it to send email, SMS and push. Users choose which channels they want. A password reset must arrive within seconds, even while a 5-million-recipient newsletter is going out.

Design the platform: 10 million notifications a day, three channels, priorities, preferences, protection from runaway callers, and no message silently lost.
functional: Internal services request notifications through one API
Deliver by email, SMS and push
Respect each user's channel preferences
nonFunctional: Urgent messages overtake bulk ones
A runaway service can't flood users
Failed deliveries are retried, then parked — never lost
A slow channel doesn't delay the others

estimate.q: What is the peak rate in notifications per second?
estimate.workings: 10M / 86,400 s ≈ 116 per second on average; × 10 at peak ≈ 1,160 per second.

tradeoff.q: Why give each channel its own queue and workers?
choices: It is required by the email provider.
Channels fail and slow down independently; separate queues stop an SMS outage from delaying email and push, and let each scale to its provider's limits.
It removes the need for priorities.
tradeoff.why: Per-channel queues are bulkheads. The cost is more queues and workers to run and monitor.

challenges.learn:
A notification platform is queues all the way down: a **rate-limited API**, a **preferences** lookup, **per-channel priority queues** with their own workers, **retries** and a **dead-letter queue**, and **idempotent** workers so retries never send twice.

The trade-off is many moving parts — worth it once dozens of services depend on it.

rules.text: Services call one notification API through a rate-limited gateway
rules.hint: A runaway service must be stopped at the door.

rules.text: The API checks user preferences
rules.hint: Which channels does each user want?

rules.text: Urgent messages overtake bulk ones
rules.hint: Look at the queues' priority option.

rules.text: Workers deliver email, SMS and push
rules.hint: Each channel needs a path from a queue through a worker to its provider.

rules.text: Each channel has its own queue
rules.hint: A slow channel must not hold up the others.

rules.text: Failed deliveries are retried, then parked
rules.hint: Retries on the queues and a dead-letter queue.

rules.text: A retried delivery is never sent twice
rules.hint: Look at the workers' properties.

rules.text: Sent notifications are logged
rules.hint: Support will ask "did the user get it?".

challenges.title: Find the weak spot
challenges.brief:
An insurance quote site promises 99.95% uptime to its partners. The architecture on the canvas has run happily for two years — but every box in it exists exactly once.

Find every single point of failure and remove it, so the loss of any one component, or a whole availability zone, doesn't take the site down.
functional: Partners request quotes
Quotes are stored
nonFunctional: No single component failure causes an outage
Survive the loss of one availability zone

estimate.q: How many minutes of downtime per 30-day month does 99.95% uptime allow?
estimate.workings: 30 × 24 × 60 = 43,200 minutes × 0.0005 = 21.6 minutes — less than one database restore.

tradeoff.q: What does removing every single point of failure cost?
choices: Nothing; redundancy is free.
Roughly double the infrastructure, plus replication and failover logic that must be tested regularly.
Slower responses for every request.
tradeoff.why: Redundancy buys availability with money and complexity. Untested failover is a hope, not a plan — rehearse it.

challenges.learn:
Walk the request path and ask of every box: **what if this dies?** The answer should be "its twin takes over" — two load balancers, several app servers, a database with a **standby**, spread across **availability zones**.

The trade-off is cost and complexity; match it to how much downtime actually costs.

challenges.title: Flaky partner
challenges.brief:
An online pharmacy books deliveries through a shipping partner's API. Every few days the partner slows to 30-second responses or drops 10% of calls. Checkout threads pile up waiting, and when the partner recovers, all the pharmacy's instant retries knock it over again.

Call the partner in a way that fails fast and retries politely.
functional: Book a delivery for each order
nonFunctional: A slow partner never ties up checkout for long
Transient failures are retried
Retries never gang up on a recovering partner

numbers.label: Partner p99 on a good day
Partner error rate on a bad day

estimate.q: If every failed call is retried 3 times immediately and the partner fails everything, how many calls per second does it receive at peak?
estimate.workings: 200 bookings/s × (1 + 3 retries) = 800 calls/s — four times normal load, exactly when it is weakest.

tradeoff.q: Why add jitter to backoff?
choices: It makes retries faster.
Without it, clients that failed together retry together in synchronised waves; random offsets spread the retries out.
Jitter reduces the number of retries to zero.
tradeoff.why: Backoff reduces the retry rate; jitter removes the synchronisation. Together they turn a thundering herd into a trickle.

challenges.learn:
Every remote call needs a **timeout** (fail fast), a small number of **retries** (for blips), **exponential backoff** (retry less and less often) and **jitter** (don't retry in lockstep).

The trade-off: retries add latency and load. Cap them, and only retry calls that are safe to repeat.

challenges.title: Break the circuit
challenges.brief:
A bookshop's product page calls a recommendations service for "you may also like". When recommendations gets slow, every product page gets slow too, then the page servers run out of threads, and the whole shop goes down — over a sidebar.

When recommendations is struggling, stop calling it and show something sensible instead.
functional: Product pages show recommendations when available
Product pages always load
nonFunctional: A failing recommendations service can't slow down product pages
Recommendations gets room to recover

estimate.q: If every call waits a 2-second timeout while recommendations is down, how many requests are stuck waiting at once?
estimate.workings: 3,000 pages/s × 2 s = 6,000 requests in flight — far more threads than the servers have.

tradeoff.q: What does a circuit breaker do once it is open?
choices: It retries the call faster.
It fails immediately without calling the dependency (usually returning a fallback), then lets a trial call through after a pause to see if it has recovered.
It restarts the dependency.
tradeoff.why: An open breaker trades a degraded answer for protecting both sides: the caller stays fast, and the dependency isn't hammered while it recovers.

challenges.learn:
A **timeout** limits how long each call can hurt you; a **circuit breaker** stops calling a dependency that keeps failing and serves a **fallback** (here, cached best-sellers).

The trade-off is a degraded experience while the breaker is open — generic recommendations instead of personal ones, but a working shop.

challenges.title: Bulkheads
challenges.brief:
An accounting SaaS runs everything through one job queue and one worker pool: payment processing, invoice PDFs, and giant CSV exports. On the first of the month, customers start hundreds of year-long exports, and payment jobs wait behind them for hours.

Isolate the workloads so exports can never starve payments.
functional: Process customer payments
Generate large CSV exports on request
nonFunctional: Payments are processed within a minute even during an export flood
Exports may be slow; payments may not

estimate.q: If all 800 exports ran on a shared pool of 20 workers, how long would the pool be busy before a payment behind them started?
estimate.workings: 800 exports × 4 min = 3,200 worker-minutes / 20 workers = 160 minutes of waiting for payments.

tradeoff.q: What does splitting into separate pools cost?
choices: Nothing.
Some capacity sits idle — export workers can't help with payments on a quiet day — so total utilisation is lower.
Payments become slower.
tradeoff.why: Bulkheads trade pooled efficiency for isolation. Autoscaling each pool separately wins back some of the waste.

challenges.learn:
**Bulkheads** give each workload its own queue and worker pool, so a flood in one compartment can't sink the others. Critical work gets reserved capacity.

The trade-off is lower utilisation — idle capacity in one pool can't help another — in exchange for predictable latency where it matters.

rules.hint: One queue per kind of work.

rules.hint: Reserve capacity per compartment, so one crashed worker doesn't stall payments.

challenges.title: Degrade gracefully
challenges.brief:
A streaming service's home page is 80% personalised rows ("Because you watched…"). When the personalization service fails, the home page shows an error and nobody can press play — even though the catalog and player are fine.

Make the home page always load: personalised when possible, a sensible default when not, and a cached copy from the edge if the origin itself is in trouble.
functional: Show a personalised home page
Show a generic home page when personalization is unavailable
nonFunctional: The home page loads even when personalization is down
The home page loads even when the origin is briefly unreachable

estimate.q: If personalization has a 150 ms budget and the rest of the page takes 250 ms, what is the worst-case page time when personalization is down?
estimate.workings: 250 ms + 150 ms timeout = 400 ms, after which the default rows are used — instead of an error.

tradeoff.q: Which of these is graceful degradation?
choices: Showing an error page until personalization recovers.
Showing generic "Top 10" rows when personalization doesn't answer in time, so users can still find something to watch.
Retrying personalization until it answers.
tradeoff.why: Degrading means keeping the core job (pick something and watch it) working with less polish. It needs the fallback designed in advance, not improvised during the outage.

challenges.learn:
**Graceful degradation** keeps the core working when extras fail: a tight **timeout** on personalization, a **fallback** (cached default rows), and a **CDN** that can serve a stale copy of the page if the origin is down.

The trade-off: a less tailored experience during failures, and fallbacks that must be tested before you need them.

rules.hint: The edge can serve a stale copy if the origin is down.

challenges.title: Shed the load
challenges.brief:
On Black Friday a department store's traffic hits 12,000 requests a second; the backend can serve 8,000. Everything slows down equally: browsing, search, and checkout all time out, and revenue drops to zero.

When overloaded, turn away the least valuable traffic first so checkout keeps working.
functional: Shoppers browse and check out
nonFunctional: Checkout keeps working at 150% of capacity
Rejected requests fail fast with a clear message

estimate.q: What share of peak traffic must be shed?
estimate.workings: (12,000 − 8,000) / 12,000 = 4,000 / 12,000 ≈ 33% — all of it can come from browsing, since checkout is only 5%.

tradeoff.q: Why reject browsing requests instead of letting every request slow down?
choices: Browsing is never important.
Slowing everything makes every request time out, including checkouts; rejecting a third of the least valuable requests keeps the rest fast.
Rejections are free for the servers.
tradeoff.why: Load shedding is triage: a fast "please retry" for some beats a slow failure for all. It needs a notion of priority, set up before the peak.

challenges.learn:
**Load shedding** rejects requests on purpose when demand exceeds capacity — **lowest priority first** — so the most valuable work stays fast. Separate fleets for checkout and browsing make the priority real.

The trade-off: some users see "try again", deliberately. Autoscaling helps with the trend, shedding with the spike.

rules.hint: One place that can decide what to reject.

challenges.title: Backups
challenges.brief:
A clinic-management SaaS stores patient records in one database. The contract says: lose at most one hour of data (RPO 1 hour), even if the whole cloud region is lost — and keep backups for ten years.

Today the only backup is a disk snapshot in the same region, taken weekly.
functional: Back up the database automatically
Restore to any hour in the last 30 days
nonFunctional: RPO of one hour
Backups survive the loss of the whole primary region
Ten-year retention at low cost

estimate.q: With an RPO of one hour, how many incremental backups (or log shipments) per day at minimum?
estimate.workings: One per hour: 24 per day. In practice, continuous log shipping plus a daily full backup.

tradeoff.q: Why store backups in another region?
choices: Other regions are cheaper.
A backup in the same region can be lost in the same disaster (or the same mistake) as the database it protects.
The law requires two regions for all data.
tradeoff.why: Backups must fail independently of what they protect. Cross-region copies cost transfer fees and a slower restore; losing both copies at once costs the company.

challenges.learn:
**RPO** sets how often you back up; **RTO** sets how fast you must restore. A scheduled job copies the database to **object storage in another region**, in a cheap tier for long retention.

The trade-off: frequent, off-site backups cost transfer and storage, and a backup you have never restored is only a hope.

challenges.title: Standby region
challenges.brief:
A logistics company's dispatch system must be back within 30 minutes if its cloud region goes down (RTO 30 minutes), losing at most a few seconds of data. Rebuilding from backups takes six hours.

Keep a warm standby in a second region that can take over quickly.
functional: Dispatchers assign trucks all day
Traffic can be switched to the standby region
nonFunctional: RTO 30 minutes
RPO a few seconds
The standby costs less than the primary while idle

estimate.q: If the standby lags the primary by 2 seconds and 150 writes happen per second, how many writes could be lost in a sudden region failure?
estimate.workings: 2 s × 150 writes/s = 300 writes — the price of asynchronous replication.

tradeoff.q: Why use asynchronous replication to the standby region?
choices: Synchronous replication is impossible between regions.
Synchronous replication would add a cross-region round trip (~70 ms) to every write; async keeps writes fast at the cost of losing the last seconds in a disaster.
Async replication never loses data.
tradeoff.why: Cross-region sync replication is possible but slow. Async trades a small RPO for normal write latency — usually the right call for a standby.

challenges.learn:
**Active-passive**: the primary region serves traffic and **replicates asynchronously** to a standby region with a smaller, warm copy of the stack. On disaster, DNS moves traffic and the standby database is promoted.

The trade-off: a few seconds of data can be lost, and the standby costs money while idle — far less than six hours of downtime.

challenges.title: Both regions live
challenges.brief:
A shared-shopping-list app is used by families in North America and Europe. With one primary region, writes from the far side take 150 ms and the app feels sluggish; and the standby region sits idle.

Serve reads and writes in both regions at once. Two family members may edit the same list in different regions at the same moment.
functional: Read and edit lists from either region
Edits made in one region appear in the other within seconds
nonFunctional: Writes are local in both regions
Either region can serve everyone if the other fails
Concurrent edits are resolved, not lost

estimate.q: If both regions each take half the 6,000 edits per second, how many replicated writes per second cross the ocean in each direction?
estimate.workings: Each region replicates its own 3,000 edits/s to the other: 3,000 per second each way.

tradeoff.q: Two people add items to the same list in different regions at the same time. What handles this best?
choices: Last write wins on the whole list — one person's item disappears.
Model the list so concurrent additions merge (for example a set of items with per-item add/remove), so both items survive.
Block writes in one region.
tradeoff.why: Active-active trades simple consistency for local latency. Data types that merge (CRDT-style) avoid losing work; last-write-wins is simpler but drops concurrent edits.

challenges.learn:
**Active-active** serves reads and writes in every region and **replicates both ways**. Latency is local and a region failure only reroutes traffic.

The price is **conflicts**: concurrent writes to the same data must be merged by rule (last-write-wins, or merge-friendly data types). Choose the rule per kind of data.

challenges.title: Never charge twice
challenges.brief:
A ride-hailing company's payment service charges riders at the end of each trip. It must keep working when an availability zone fails, when the card processor is flaky, and when phones on bad networks resend the same request five times.

A rider must be charged exactly once per trip, and every successful charge must reliably trigger the receipt and driver payout — even if the service crashes right after charging.
functional: Charge the rider at the end of each trip
Send a receipt and schedule the driver payout after each successful charge
nonFunctional: Never charge twice for one trip
Survive the loss of one availability zone
Flaky processor calls are retried safely, and a failing processor is not hammered
A charge and its "charged" event never diverge

numbers.label: Processor timeout rate on bad days

estimate.q: At a 2% resend rate, how many duplicate charge requests arrive per day?
estimate.workings: 3,000,000 trips × 0.02 = 60,000 duplicates a day, each of which must be recognised.

tradeoff.q: Why use an outbox instead of publishing the "charged" event right after the database commit?
choices: Publishing is slower than writing a row.
If the service crashes between the commit and the publish, the rider is charged but no receipt or payout ever happens; the outbox makes both part of one transaction.
Events can't be published from payment services.
tradeoff.why: Two separate writes (database, then broker) can fail halfway. The outbox writes the event in the same transaction as the charge, and a relay publishes it later — at least once, so consumers dedupe too.

challenges.learn:
Money flows combine every reliability tool: **idempotency keys** so resends are recognised, **retries with backoff and jitter** plus a **circuit breaker** on the processor, a **multi-AZ database**, and a **transactional outbox** so a charge and its event never diverge.

The trade-off is complexity everywhere — justified because a double charge or a lost payout costs trust, not just money.

challenges.title: Read your writes
challenges.brief:
A professional profile site sends reads to replicas that lag up to two seconds. When people edit their headline and press save, the page reloads showing the old headline, so they edit again — and file bug reports.

Other visitors may see the change a moment later. The person who made it must see it immediately.
functional: Members edit their profile
Everyone reads profiles
nonFunctional: A member always sees their own edits right away
Most reads still go to replicas

estimate.q: 1,000 members save an edit every minute, and each then makes 3 reads within 5 seconds. How many extra reads per second go to the primary?
estimate.workings: 1,000 / 60 s ≈ 16.7 edits per second × 3 reads = 50 reads/s on the primary — against tens of thousands on the replicas.

tradeoff.q: Which approach gives read-your-writes without sending all reads to the primary?
choices: Make replication synchronous for everyone.
Remember when each user last wrote (for example in a session store) and route that user's reads to the primary for a few seconds afterwards.
Tell users to wait before refreshing.
tradeoff.why: Session-based routing keeps the cheap, scalable replica reads for almost everyone and pays for the primary only when it matters. The cost is a little routing logic and state per user.

challenges.learn:
**Read-your-writes** is a per-user guarantee: route a user's reads to the primary for a short time after they write (tracked in a session store), and everyone else keeps reading from replicas.

The trade-off is a bit of extra state and routing logic, instead of paying for strong consistency everywhere.

challenges.title: Quorum
challenges.brief:
A game company stores player inventories in a leaderless key-value store with three copies of every key. With the current settings (write to one copy, read from one copy), players sometimes see an item they just bought disappear on the next screen.

Choose quorum settings so every read sees the latest write, while one copy can be down without blocking reads or writes.
functional: Store player inventories
Read an inventory right after changing it
nonFunctional: Every read returns the latest acknowledged write
One copy can be down without blocking reads or writes

estimate.q: With N = 3, R = 2, W = 2, how many copies can be down while reads and writes still succeed?
estimate.workings: Reads need 2 of 3 and writes need 2 of 3, so both still work with 1 copy down; with 2 down, neither does.

tradeoff.q: Why not use R = 3 and W = 3?
choices: It is inconsistent.
It is consistent, but any single copy being down blocks every read and write, and every request waits for the slowest copy.
It uses less storage.
tradeoff.why: Quorums trade latency and availability for consistency. R = W = 2 with N = 3 is the classic balance: consistent, and tolerant of one failure.

challenges.learn:
With **N** copies, reading **R** and writing **W** copies guarantees overlap when **R + W > N** — so a read always includes the latest write. N = 3, R = 2, W = 2 stays consistent with one copy down.

The trade-off: every request waits for more than one copy, so latency follows the second-fastest replica.

rules.hint: Set N on the key-value store.

rules.hint: Pick R and W so that R + W > N.

challenges.title: One leader
challenges.brief:
A payroll company runs a scheduler that starts salary payments at midnight. It runs on one machine — a single point of failure — but when they tried running three copies, salaries were paid three times.

Run several schedulers for safety, but make sure exactly one of them is in charge at any moment.
functional: Start payroll jobs on schedule
nonFunctional: Jobs start even if a scheduler machine dies
A job is never started by two schedulers at once

estimate.q: With a 10-second lease, what is the longest gap before a new leader takes over after the old one dies?
estimate.workings: The old lease must expire first: up to 10 s, then another scheduler acquires it. Shorter leases mean faster takeover but more coordination traffic.

tradeoff.q: Why use a coordination service (like ZooKeeper or etcd) for leader election instead of a flag in the application database?
choices: Databases can't store flags.
A coordination service is built for consensus: leases that expire when a leader dies and strong guarantees that two nodes never both believe they lead.
It is faster at storing payroll data.
tradeoff.why: Leader election is subtle (network partitions, paused processes). A consensus-based service with leases handles those cases; the leader should also pass a fencing token so a stale leader's actions are rejected.

challenges.learn:
Run several schedulers for availability, and use **leader election** on a **coordination service** so only one acts at a time. When the leader's lease expires, another takes over.

The trade-off: failover isn't instant (up to one lease), and you run a consensus cluster. Workers should still be idempotent in case a paused old leader wakes up.

rules.hint: One is a single point of failure.

challenges.title: Last item
challenges.brief:
A vintage-furniture shop sells one-of-a-kind pieces. Twice this month, two customers bought the same armchair within the same second: both checkouts read "in stock", both wrote "sold", and one customer got an apology email.

Make sure only one buyer can win the last item, even with many app servers checking out in parallel.
functional: Customers buy unique items
nonFunctional: An item is never sold twice
Checkout of different items isn't slowed down

estimate.q: Two checkouts each take 120 ms between reading stock and writing "sold". How long is the window in which a second buyer can sneak in?
estimate.workings: Any checkout starting within the other's 120 ms read-to-write gap can read the same "in stock" — the race window.

tradeoff.q: When is optimistic locking a better fit than pessimistic locking?
choices: When conflicts are rare: nothing is locked, and the rare loser simply retries or is told the item is gone.
When conflicts are constant.
Never; pessimistic locking is always better.
tradeoff.why: Optimistic locking (check a version at write time) costs nothing when there is no conflict. Pessimistic locking (lock the row first) is better when many writers fight over the same rows.

challenges.learn:
A race between "check" and "update" needs **concurrency control**: a database row lock (**pessimistic**), a version check at write time (**optimistic**), or a **distributed lock** when the work spans more than one database.

The trade-off: locks add waiting under contention; optimistic checks add retries. Both beat an apology email.

rules.hint: The stock lives somewhere.

challenges.title: Two-phase commit
challenges.brief:
A credit union keeps savings accounts and loan accounts in two separate databases run by different teams. A loan repayment must debit savings and credit the loan together: if either side fails, neither may happen.

Both databases support prepare/commit. Make the transfer atomic across them.
functional: Transfer money from a savings account to a loan account
nonFunctional: Both sides commit, or neither does
No money appears or disappears, even if a database fails mid-way

estimate.q: 2PC needs two round trips to each database (prepare, then commit). With 5 ms per round trip, done in parallel for both databases, how long is the commit protocol?
estimate.workings: Two phases × 5 ms = 10 ms, during which the rows stay locked.

tradeoff.q: What is the main weakness of two-phase commit?
choices: It can't involve more than one database.
If the coordinator fails after "prepare", participants hold locks and can't decide on their own; the transaction blocks until the coordinator recovers.
It sometimes commits only one side.
tradeoff.why: 2PC gives atomicity across databases at the cost of availability: prepared participants wait for the coordinator. It suits low-volume, high-value operations inside one organisation; sagas suit the rest.

challenges.learn:
**Two-phase commit**: a coordinator asks every participant to **prepare** (promise it can commit), then tells them all to **commit** — or all to abort.

The trade-off is blocking: locks are held across both phases, and a coordinator crash leaves participants waiting. Use it sparingly, for a few databases that must agree.

rules.hint: Start from the member.

rules.text: Transfers run through a transaction coordinator
rules.hint: Something must drive prepare and commit.

rules.text: The coordinator talks to both databases
rules.hint: Connect the coordinator to each participant.

rules.text: Savings and loans stay in separate databases
rules.hint: Two databases, owned by two teams.

rules.text: Balances use serializable isolation
rules.hint: Transfers must behave as if they ran one at a time.

rules.hint: A direct write isn't part of the atomic transfer.

challenges.title: Saga: choreography
challenges.brief:
A travel site sells packages: flight, hotel and car, each booked by a separate service with its own database. 2PC across three partners is not an option. If the car can't be booked, the hotel and flight must be cancelled.

Let the services coordinate through events alone — no central controller.
functional: Book a flight, a hotel and a car as one package
If any step fails, undo the steps already done
nonFunctional: No service calls another directly
Each service owns its data

estimate.q: At a 4% car failure rate, how many packages per hour need compensations?
estimate.workings: 3,000 × 0.04 = 120 packages whose flight and hotel must be cancelled each hour.

tradeoff.q: What is the main downside of choreography?
choices: Services are tightly coupled.
The overall flow isn't written down anywhere — it emerges from who listens to what — so it is hard to see, test and change as steps grow.
It needs two-phase commit.
tradeoff.why: Choreography keeps services independent and is great for a few steps. With many steps, the implicit flow and cyclic event dependencies become hard to follow; orchestration makes the flow explicit.

challenges.learn:
A **saga** replaces one big transaction with local steps plus **compensations**. In **choreography**, each service reacts to events ("hotel booked" → book the car; "car failed" → cancel the hotel).

The trade-off: no central place shows the flow, and the system is only **eventually** consistent — a customer may briefly hold a hotel that is about to be cancelled.

rules.text: Services communicate through events
rules.hint: Add an event stream or topic they all use.

rules.text: The booking service starts the saga with an event
rules.hint: It publishes "package requested".

rules.text: Flight, hotel and car services react to events
rules.hint: Each consumes from the event channel.

rules.text: A failed car booking reaches the hotel and flight services
rules.hint: The car service publishes its result so the others can compensate.

rules.text: Each step service owns its data
rules.hint: A database per service.

rules.text: Services don't call each other directly
rules.hint: Direct calls turn choreography back into a tangle of dependencies.

rules.hint: That's the next challenge.

challenges.title: Saga: orchestration
challenges.brief:
An electronics retailer's order process has five steps: reserve stock, charge payment, create shipment, send confirmation, and update loyalty points. Each is a separate service. Choreography got out of hand — nobody can say what happens after a failed shipment.

Put one component in charge of the flow, its state and its compensations.
functional: Run the five order steps in order
On failure, run the compensations for completed steps
nonFunctional: The flow is defined in one place
A crash mid-order resumes where it left off
Retried steps don't repeat side effects

estimate.q: If the steps run one after another, how long does an order take end to end?
estimate.workings: 5 steps × 150 ms = 750 ms (plus the orchestrator's own bookkeeping).

tradeoff.q: What must the orchestrator store durably?
choices: Nothing; it can keep state in memory.
Each saga's current step and outcome, so a restarted orchestrator knows which steps to continue or compensate.
The whole product catalog.
tradeoff.why: An orchestrator is only reliable if its state survives crashes. The cost is a write per step; the benefit is a flow you can read, monitor and resume.

challenges.learn:
In **orchestration**, a central **orchestrator** calls each step, records progress, and runs compensations in reverse on failure. The flow is explicit and easy to change.

The trade-off: the orchestrator is a critical component (it needs durable state and redundancy), and services must be **idempotent** because steps may be retried.

rules.hint: Something drives the flow.

rules.text: The orchestrator drives each step
rules.hint: Connect the orchestrator to every step service.

rules.text: Saga state is stored durably
rules.hint: Where does the orchestrator record each order's progress?

rules.text: Payment is charged through the provider
rules.hint: Who moves the money?

rules.text: Step services are idempotent
rules.hint: Retries must not double-charge or double-ship.

rules.text: Step calls are retried with backoff
rules.hint: Transient failures shouldn't trigger compensation right away.

rules.text: Step services don't call each other
rules.hint: Hidden calls between services bring back the tangle.

challenges.title: Transactional outbox
challenges.brief:
A marketplace's order service saves each order to its database and then publishes "order created" to a stream for warehouses. Once a week the service crashes between the two, and an order exists that no warehouse ever hears about. Publishing first is worse: warehouses ship orders that were never saved.

Make saving and publishing succeed or fail together.
functional: Save orders
Publish an "order created" event for every saved order
nonFunctional: Never a saved order without its event, or an event without its order
The order service stays fast

estimate.q: If the relay polls the outbox every 200 ms, what is the worst-case extra delay before an event is published?
estimate.workings: An event written just after a poll waits a full interval: up to 200 ms. CDC on the database log can cut this further.

tradeoff.q: The relay publishes an event and crashes before marking it sent. What happens?
choices: The event is lost.
It publishes the event again after restarting, so consumers must handle duplicates — the outbox gives at-least-once delivery.
The order is deleted.
tradeoff.why: The outbox guarantees the event is eventually published, not that it is published exactly once. Consumers dedupe by event ID.

challenges.learn:
The **transactional outbox**: write the order **and** the event row in the same database transaction; a **relay** (or a **CDC** connector reading the log) publishes outbox rows to the stream.

The trade-off: a small publishing delay and at-least-once delivery, so consumers must deduplicate — in exchange for never losing or inventing an event.

rules.hint: Start from the order service.

rules.text: A relay reads the outbox from the database
rules.hint: An outbox relay or CDC connector connected to the database.

rules.text: The relay publishes to the stream
rules.hint: Connect the relay to the event stream.

rules.text: Warehouses consume the events
rules.hint: Who reacts to "order created"?

rules.text: Warehouses handle duplicate events
rules.hint: Delivery is at-least-once.

rules.hint: Writing to the database and the stream separately is the "dual write" that caused the problem.

challenges.title: CQRS
challenges.brief:
A project-management tool's write database also serves management dashboards: "tasks per team per week", "overdue by customer". The dashboard queries scan millions of rows and lock tables, and task updates time out every Monday morning.

Separate the write model from the read models, and keep the read models up to date from changes.
functional: Teams create and update tasks
Managers view dashboards with rolled-up numbers
nonFunctional: Dashboard queries never slow down task updates
Dashboards are at most a few seconds behind

estimate.q: If each dashboard query scanned 5M rows at 10M rows/s on the write database, how many seconds of database time do 6,000 queries per minute need, per second?
estimate.workings: 5M / 10M = 0.5 s per query; 6,000 per minute = 100 per second × 0.5 s = 50 seconds of work every second — impossible on one database.

tradeoff.q: What do dashboard users give up with CQRS?
choices: Nothing.
Immediate consistency: a task updated a moment ago may not be in the numbers yet, because projections are updated asynchronously.
The ability to see any data at all.
tradeoff.why: CQRS trades freshness for isolation and speed. Each read model is shaped for its queries and can be rebuilt from events; the write model stays lean.

challenges.learn:
**CQRS** splits commands from queries: writes go to a model built for correctness; changes flow (here via **CDC** and a stream) into **projections** shaped for each dashboard.

The trade-off is **eventual consistency** and more moving parts; the gain is that reads and writes scale — and fail — independently.

rules.text: Task updates go to the write database
rules.hint: Start from the team member.

rules.text: Changes flow from the write database into a stream
rules.hint: CDC or an outbox relay from the database to a stream.

rules.text: A projector builds a separate read model
rules.hint: Something consumes the changes and writes a store shaped for dashboards.

rules.text: Dashboards read from the read model
rules.hint: Dashboards query the projection, not the write database.

rules.text: More than one projection
rules.hint: Different dashboards may want different shapes; a search index is another projection.

rules.text: Dashboards don't query the write database
rules.hint: That is exactly the load you are removing.

challenges.title: Bank ledger
challenges.brief:
A digital bank needs its core ledger. Every movement of money must be recorded exactly once and never edited — corrections are new entries. Balances must be strongly consistent when money moves, but the app shows balances to millions of users who open it all day. Auditors must be able to replay every entry for seven years.

Design the ledger, its balance views and its audit trail.
functional: Post transfers between accounts
Show balances and statements in the app
Give auditors the complete, replayable history
nonFunctional: Entries are never updated or deleted
No transfer is applied twice
Postings behave as if run one at a time
Balance reads don't load the ledger

estimate.q: Each transfer writes 2 entries (debit and credit) of 300 bytes. How much ledger data per year at an average of 500 transfers/s?
estimate.workings: 500 × 2 × 300 bytes = 300 KB/s × 31.5M s/year ≈ 9.5 TB per year.

tradeoff.q: Why is the ledger append-only instead of updating a balance column?
choices: Updates are not supported by SQL.
Every change stays on record, so balances can be recomputed, audited and explained; a mistake is fixed by a new correcting entry, not by rewriting history.
Append-only tables use less disk.
tradeoff.why: Append-only costs more storage and needs projections for fast balance reads. It buys a complete audit trail and the ability to rebuild any view from the entries.

challenges.learn:
A ledger is **append-only**: entries are never edited, and balances are **projections** of them. Postings run in **serializable** transactions and are **idempotent** by transfer ID. Balance reads go to a separate read model (CQRS), and the entry stream is archived for auditors.

The trade-off is complexity and storage — the price of money you can always explain.

rules.hint: Start from the customer.

rules.hint: Look at the ledger database's properties.

rules.hint: The ledger database's isolation level.

rules.hint: A balances service reads a read model built from the stream.

rules.hint: Archive the stream to long-term storage.

rules.hint: Replicate the ledger database to a standby.

rules.text: Ledger data is encrypted with managed keys
rules.hint: Key management for the ledger.

rules.text: The archive uses a cheap, long-term tier
rules.hint: Seven years of audit data.

challenges.title: Strangler fig
challenges.brief:
An insurer's ten-year-old monolith does everything, and nobody dares touch it. The team wants to move billing into a new service first, then other parts over the next two years — without a big-bang cut-over and without clients noticing.

The current design is on the canvas. Put something in front that can send billing routes to the new service and everything else to the monolith.
functional: Billing requests are served by the new billing service
Everything else is still served by the monolith
nonFunctional: Clients keep using the same address
Routes can be moved one at a time and moved back if needed

estimate.q: At 35 routes migrated per quarter, how many quarters until all ~400 routes have moved?
estimate.workings: 400 / 35 ≈ 11.4 quarters — close to three years, so the gateway will live for a long time.

tradeoff.q: What is the main risk of the strangler approach?
choices: It requires rewriting everything at once.
For a long time you run two systems, and data both use (like customer records) must be kept in sync or accessed through one owner.
Clients must change their URLs.
tradeoff.why: Incremental migration trades a risky big bang for a long period of coexistence. Plan the data ownership early — shared data is where migrations stall.

challenges.learn:
The **strangler fig** pattern puts a router (an **API gateway**) in front of the monolith. Migrated routes go to new services; everything else still reaches the monolith. Each move is small and reversible.

The trade-off is running two systems side by side for a long time, with careful handling of the data they share.

rules.text: Clients reach everything through a gateway
rules.hint: One front door that knows which routes have moved.

rules.text: Unmigrated routes still reach the monolith
rules.hint: Keep the monolith behind the gateway.

rules.text: Billing routes go to the new billing service
rules.hint: Add the new service behind the gateway.

rules.text: No client reaches the monolith around the gateway
rules.hint: Everything goes through the router, or routes can't be moved.

rules.text: The billing service has its own database
rules.hint: Don't let the new service depend on the monolith's schema.

challenges.title: Own your data
challenges.brief:
A food-delivery startup split its monolith into orders, users and inventory services — but all three still read and write the same database. A column rename in the users table broke checkout last week, and no team can deploy alone.

The current design is on the canvas. Give each service its own data, and let them share information another way.
functional: Each service manages its own entities
Orders can still show the customer's name and check stock
nonFunctional: A schema change in one service can't break another
Teams deploy independently

estimate.q: If each of the 17 cross-service joins must become an API call or a copied field, and each takes about 3 developer-days, how many developer-days is the migration?
estimate.workings: 17 × 3 = 51 developer-days — the real cost of a shared database is paid on the way out.

tradeoff.q: Orders needs the customer's name. Without a shared database, what are the options?
choices: There are none; it must read the users table.
Ask the users service's API when needed, or keep a local copy updated from "user changed" events.
Store the name in the gateway.
tradeoff.why: Owning data means other services get it through an API (fresh, but a runtime dependency) or events (independent, but eventually consistent). Joins across services disappear.

challenges.learn:
**Database per service**: each service is the only one touching its store, and shares data through its API or its **events**. Schema changes stay private, so teams can deploy alone.

The trade-off: no cross-service joins or transactions; you get eventual consistency and duplicated read models instead.

rules.text: Every service has a store of its own
rules.hint: Connect each service to its own database.

rules.text: No database is shared between services
rules.hint: Three services, three stores — and no extra connections into another service's store.

rules.text: Clients still reach every service through the gateway
rules.hint: Keep the gateway routes.

rules.text: Services share changes through events
rules.hint: Users publishes "user changed"; orders keeps what it needs.

challenges.title: Where's my service?
challenges.brief:
A ride-booking platform autoscales its pricing service from 4 to 40 instances during rush hour. The callers use a hard-coded list of addresses, so new instances get no traffic and requests keep going to instances that were shut down.

Let instances announce themselves and let callers find the healthy ones.
functional: New instances receive traffic within seconds
Stopped instances stop receiving traffic
nonFunctional: No hard-coded addresses
Discovery keeps working if one registry node fails

estimate.q: With a 10-second heartbeat and 3 missed heartbeats before removal, how long can a dead instance stay listed?
estimate.workings: 3 × 10 s = 30 s; callers should still time out and retry on another instance.

tradeoff.q: What should a caller do if the registry is briefly unreachable?
choices: Fail every request.
Keep using its last known list of instances (a local cache) and refresh when the registry is back.
Call a random IP address.
tradeoff.why: The registry is on every call path, so callers cache its answers. The trade-off is acting on slightly stale lists — timeouts and retries cover that.

challenges.learn:
**Service discovery**: instances **register** in a service registry and send heartbeats; callers **look up** healthy instances (and cache the list). Autoscaling then just works.

The trade-off is another critical component: the registry must be replicated, and callers must tolerate slightly stale answers.

rules.hint: Add a registry.

rules.text: Pricing instances register themselves
rules.hint: Connect the pricing service to the registry.

rules.text: Callers look up pricing instances in the registry
rules.hint: The booking service asks the registry before calling.

rules.hint: The actual call.

rules.hint: It autoscales from 4 upwards.

challenges.title: Encrypt the inside
challenges.brief:
A health-insurance company terminates HTTPS at its gateway, but the calls between its thirty internal services travel in clear text. An audit flags it: anyone who gets onto the internal network can read claims data, and any process can pretend to be any service.

Encrypt and authenticate every service-to-service call, without changing each service's code.
functional: Services keep calling each other as today
nonFunctional: Every internal call is encrypted
Each side proves its identity
No application code changes

estimate.q: With 30 services × 3 instances each and certificates rotated daily, how many certificates does the control plane issue per day?
estimate.workings: 30 × 3 = 90 sidecars, each getting a new 24-hour certificate every day.

tradeoff.q: What does a sidecar-based mesh cost?
choices: Nothing.
An extra proxy hop (a little latency and CPU) on every call, plus a control plane to run and upgrade.
Services must be rewritten.
tradeoff.why: Sidecars move security and networking out of application code. You pay a small per-call overhead and operate the mesh — usually cheaper than implementing mTLS in thirty codebases.

challenges.learn:
A **service mesh** puts a **sidecar** proxy next to each service. A **control plane** issues short-lived certificates and configures the sidecars so every call uses **mutual TLS**: encrypted, with both sides authenticated.

The trade-off is an extra hop per call and another platform to operate — but no application code changes.

rules.hint: Keep the internal calls.

rules.text: Every service runs a sidecar proxy
rules.hint: Look at each service's properties.

rules.text: A mesh control plane enforces mutual TLS
rules.hint: Add a control plane and turn on mTLS.

rules.text: The control plane configures every service's sidecar
rules.hint: Connect the control plane to the services.

rules.text: External traffic also arrives encrypted
rules.hint: The gateway already terminates HTTPS; keep clients behind it.

rules.text: Sidecars report traces
rules.hint: Meshes make tracing almost free.

challenges.title: Who are you?
challenges.brief:
A company has four internal apps — HR, expenses, wiki and helpdesk — each with its own login page and password database. Staff reuse passwords, leavers keep access for weeks, and every app implements login slightly wrong.

Let staff sign in once, and let the gateway verify who is calling before requests reach any app.
functional: Staff sign in once for all apps
Every API request carries proof of who is calling
nonFunctional: Apps never see passwords
Revoking a user in one place removes access everywhere
Verifying a request doesn't call the identity provider every time

estimate.q: With 1-hour tokens, how many token refreshes per second do 8,000 active staff cause?
estimate.workings: 8,000 users / 3,600 s ≈ 2.2 per second — tiny next to 3,000 requests/s that are verified locally.

tradeoff.q: Why can the gateway verify a JWT without calling the identity provider?
choices: It can't; every request must call the identity provider.
The token is signed; the gateway checks the signature with the provider's public key, which it fetches occasionally and caches.
JWTs are encrypted with the user's password.
tradeoff.why: Self-contained tokens make verification local and fast. The trade-off: a token stays valid until it expires, so lifetimes are kept short (minutes to an hour).

challenges.learn:
**Single sign-on**: users log in at an **identity provider** (OIDC), which issues signed **JWTs**. The **API gateway** verifies the signature on every request using the provider's cached public keys, and apps trust the verified identity.

The trade-off: tokens can't be revoked instantly — keep them short-lived.

rules.hint: One place for passwords and login.

rules.hint: Look at the identity provider's protocol and token type.

rules.hint: Turn on auth at the gateway.

challenges.title: No secrets in code
challenges.brief:
A security scan of a travel agency's repository found the production database password, the payment provider's API key and an encryption key committed in config files — readable by every contractor who ever had access.

Move every secret out of code, fetch them at runtime, and keep the encryption keys where nobody can copy them.
functional: Apps get the database password and API keys at startup
Sensitive fields (passport numbers) are encrypted
nonFunctional: No secret in code, config files or images
Secrets can be rotated without a deploy
Encryption keys never leave the key service

estimate.q: With 60 secrets rotated every 90 days, about how many rotations happen per week?
estimate.workings: 60 / 90 days ≈ 0.67 per day × 7 ≈ 4.7 per week — only practical if rotation is automated.

tradeoff.q: Why use a KMS for encryption keys instead of storing them in the secrets manager too?
choices: The secrets manager can't store long strings.
With a KMS the key never leaves it: apps send data to be encrypted or decrypted, so even a compromised app can't copy the key.
KMS keys never need rotating.
tradeoff.why: Secrets managers hand secrets out; a KMS performs the crypto itself. The trade-off is a network call per operation — often reduced with envelope encryption (the KMS encrypts per-record data keys).

challenges.learn:
A **secrets manager** stores passwords and API keys, hands them to services at runtime, and rotates them. A **KMS** holds encryption keys and does the encryption itself, so keys never leave it. The secrets manager usually encrypts its own store with a KMS key.

The trade-off: startup depends on these services, so they must be highly available.

rules.hint: Where does the database password come from now?

rules.hint: The secrets manager's own storage is protected by the KMS.

challenges.title: Private by default
challenges.brief:
A penetration test on an e-commerce site found the database answering on a public IP, and the app servers reachable directly from the internet, bypassing the load balancer and its protections.

The current design is on the canvas. Place everything in a private network so that only the load balancer faces the internet.
