nonFunctional: Only the load balancer is reachable from the internet
App servers and the database have no public exposure

estimate.q: Before the fix, the load balancer, two app servers and the database were all reachable. How many internet-facing entry points does the fix remove?
estimate.workings: 4 exposed components − 1 load balancer that must stay public = 3 fewer ways in.

tradeoff.q: App servers in private subnets still need to call a payment provider on the internet. How?
choices: Move them to the public subnet.
Through a NAT gateway: outbound connections are allowed, inbound ones are not.
They can't; payments must move to the load balancer.
tradeoff.why: Private subnets block inbound traffic, not outbound. Segmentation shrinks the attack surface at the cost of a bit of network plumbing (NAT, security groups).

challenges.learn:
**Network segmentation**: only the entry point (load balancer) sits in a **public subnet**; app servers and databases live in **private subnets** inside a **VPC**, reachable only from inside.

The trade-off is network plumbing — NAT for outbound calls, bastions or VPN for admin access — for a much smaller attack surface.

rules.hint: Draw a VPC around the load balancer, app servers and database.

rules.hint: Not reachable from the internet.

challenges.title: See the system
challenges.brief:
A food-ordering app learns about outages from angry tweets. Last Friday, 20% of orders failed for two hours before anyone at the company noticed. Logs exist, but they sit on each server and disappear when servers are replaced.

Collect logs and metrics centrally, show them on dashboards, and wake someone up when things go wrong.
functional: Search logs from all servers in one place
See error rate and latency on a dashboard
Page the on-call engineer when the error rate spikes
nonFunctional: Problems are detected within minutes, before customers report them
Logs survive server replacement

estimate.q: If orders fail at 20% of 300 orders per minute for 2 hours, how many failed orders is that?
estimate.workings: 300 × 0.2 = 60 failed orders per minute × 120 minutes = 7,200 — detecting in 5 minutes would have cut this to 300.

tradeoff.q: What makes a good alert?
choices: Alert on every error log line.
Alert on symptoms users feel (error rate, latency) crossing a threshold for a few minutes, so every page is real and actionable.
Alert only once a day.
tradeoff.why: Noisy alerts get ignored. Symptom-based alerts page less often and matter more; detailed causes live in logs and dashboards for investigation.

challenges.learn:
**Observability** starts with three signals: **logs** gathered centrally, **metrics** (rates, errors, latency) in a metrics store, and **alerts** on user-facing symptoms. **Dashboards** show the trends.

The trade-off is cost — log volume adds up fast — and alert tuning: too many pages and people stop reacting.

rules.hint: Logs shouldn't die with the server.

rules.text: Services report metrics
rules.hint: Error rate and latency need a metrics store.

rules.hint: Connect metrics to alerting.

rules.hint: Page by SMS, push or email.

rules.text: Dashboards show the metrics
rules.hint: Trends at a glance.

rules.hint: Keep old logs for investigations without paying hot prices.

challenges.title: Trace it
challenges.brief:
Checkout at an online bookstore takes 4 seconds at p99. It passes through five services, each of whose dashboards says "I'm fast". Nobody can tell where the time actually goes for a single slow request.

Follow each checkout request across every service it touches.
functional: See the full path and timing of any single request
Find the slowest step of slow checkouts
nonFunctional: Every service reports its part of each request
Tracing overhead stays small

estimate.q: At 10% sampling, how many traces per second are stored, and each has 5 spans — how many spans per second?
estimate.workings: 200 × 0.1 = 20 traces per second × 5 spans = 100 spans per second.

tradeoff.q: Why sample traces instead of recording every request?
choices: Sampling makes requests faster.
Full tracing of every request costs a lot of storage and some CPU; a sample (plus keeping all errors and slow requests) is enough to see patterns.
Tracing is only allowed on 10% of requests.
tradeoff.why: Sampling trades completeness for cost. Tail-based sampling keeps the interesting traces (errors, slow ones) even at low rates.

challenges.learn:

The trade-off: every service must propagate the ID (a mesh or library helps), and storage grows with traffic, so traces are sampled.

challenges.title: Online store
challenges.brief:
A growing sportswear brand is replacing its storefront monolith with services: catalog, cart, order, payment and inventory. Customers log in with their account. When an order is placed, inventory must be reserved and the payment taken; the teams want to deploy independently and to know about problems before customers do.

Design the whole store.

Keep a cart
Place an order, reserve stock and take payment
Customers log in
nonFunctional: Each service owns its data

estimate.q: If 0.2% of 5,000 peak requests per second are "place order", how many order events per second hit the stream?
estimate.workings: 5,000 × 0.002 = 10 order events per second at peak — about 4× the daily average of 200,000 / 86,400 s ≈ 2.3 per second. Browsing, not ordering, drives the request load.

tradeoff.q: Placing an order involves order, inventory and payment. Why events instead of a distributed transaction?
choices: Events are always faster than transactions.
Each service keeps its own database and availability; the order moves through states (pending → reserved → paid) with compensations if a step fails, instead of locking three databases together.
Distributed transactions can't include payments at all.
tradeoff.why: Event-driven sagas keep services independent at the cost of eventual consistency: an order can be "pending" for a moment, and failures need compensations.

challenges.learn:
A microservice store brings the chapter together: an **authenticating gateway** backed by an identity provider, **a database per service**, **events** between order, inventory and payment, secrets out of code, and **metrics with alerting**.

The trade-off is operational weight — many services, stores and pipelines — in exchange for teams that ship independently and failures that stay contained.

challenges.title: Find it
challenges.brief:
A home-improvement store's product search runs `LIKE '%drill%'` on the product table. It takes three seconds, can't rank results, and misses "drils". Worse, the team once wrote products to a search engine from the app too, and the two copies drifted apart.

Add real search, kept in sync from the database automatically.
functional: Keyword search with ranking and typo tolerance
Filters by category, brand and price
nonFunctional: Search under 100 ms
Product changes appear in search within seconds
Search never drifts from the database

estimate.q: With 50,000 updates a day, how many index updates per second does the sync handle on average?
estimate.workings: 50,000 / 86,400 s ≈ 0.58 per second — trivial, but it must never miss one.

tradeoff.q: Why feed the index with CDC rather than writing to it from the app?
choices: The app can't talk to search engines.
CDC reads every committed change from the database log, so the index can't miss or invent changes the way two separate writes from the app can.
CDC makes searches faster.
tradeoff.why: Two writes from the app (database, then index) can diverge on any failure. CDC derives the index from the source of truth; the cost is a small indexing delay and another pipeline to run.

challenges.learn:
A **search index** is a read-optimised copy of your data. Feed it with **change data capture** from the database, through a stream, so it can always be rebuilt and never drifts.

The trade-off: search is **eventually consistent** — a price change shows in search a second or two later.

challenges.title: Autocomplete
challenges.brief:
A travel search site wants suggestions as people type — "par" → Paris, Parma, Paraty — ranked by popularity, in under 50 ms. Every keystroke is a request, and the list of popular searches changes daily.

nonFunctional: p99 under 50 ms

estimate.q: How many suggestion requests per second on average?
estimate.workings: 10M searches × 8 keystrokes = 80M requests / 86,400 s ≈ 926 per second (several times that at peak).

tradeoff.q: Why precompute the top suggestions per prefix instead of searching at request time?
choices: Precomputing is always more accurate.
A lookup by prefix is a single key read, easily cached; searching and ranking at every keystroke would blow the 50 ms budget.
Search indexes can't handle prefixes.
tradeoff.why: Precomputed prefix → top-10 tables turn a search into a key lookup. The cost is freshness: new trends appear only after the next rebuild (or a separate fast-trending path).

challenges.learn:
**Typeahead** is a read-heavy key lookup: a **batch job** builds prefix → top suggestions from search logs, a **store** holds them, and a **cache** (and even the CDN) serves the hottest prefixes.

The trade-off is freshness — suggestions lag behind trends until the next build.

challenges.title: Nightly numbers
challenges.brief:
An e-commerce company's finance team runs revenue reports straight against the production database. The queries scan years of orders; checkout slows to a crawl every time someone opens the monthly report.

Move analytics to a warehouse, loaded every night, and keep heavy reads off the primary.

estimate.workings: 200,000 × 365 × 6 ≈ 438,000,000 rows — a job for a columnar warehouse, not the checkout database.

tradeoff.q: What does finance give up with a nightly batch?
choices: Accuracy.
Freshness: today's orders appear tomorrow. Near-real-time needs streaming, at more cost and complexity.
The ability to query more than one year.
tradeoff.why: Nightly ETL is simple, cheap and isolates production. If "yesterday" is fresh enough for reports, it is the right choice.

challenges.learn:
**ETL**: a scheduled batch job **extracts** from the operational database (ideally from a replica), **transforms** it and **loads** a **data warehouse** built for analytics.

The trade-off is freshness — data is as old as the last run — in exchange for isolating analytics from customer traffic.

A grocery-delivery company wants a wall screen in the operations room showing orders per minute for each city, updated every few seconds. The nightly warehouse is a day late; querying the orders database every five seconds would hurt checkout.

Count it in the current minute.
tradeoff.why: Windows over event time handle late data up to a limit; beyond it you trade completeness for timely results. Tumbling windows are simple; sliding windows smooth the curve at more cost.

**Stream processing**: the order service publishes events; a **stream processor** groups them into **windows** (per city, per minute) and writes the results to a **time-series database** that the dashboard reads.

The trade-off: results are approximate for late events, and you run a stateful streaming job.

challenges.title: Keep everything
challenges.brief:
A media company's data scientists want every raw click, scroll and play event kept forever, in its original form, so they can answer questions nobody has thought of yet. Analysts also want tidy daily tables for dashboards.

Collect the clickstream, keep it raw and cheap, and process it in batches into analytics tables.

Raw storage cost stays low as data grows
Any day can be reprocessed from raw data

tradeoff.q: Why keep raw events in a data lake instead of only the aggregated tables?
choices: Raw events are smaller.
Aggregates answer only the questions you planned; raw events can be reprocessed for new questions and to fix bugs in old pipelines.
Warehouses can't store numbers.
tradeoff.why: A lake is cheap storage with schema on read — flexible, but raw data is messy and needs processing before most people can use it.

challenges.learn:
A **data lake** keeps raw events cheaply and indefinitely; **batch jobs** turn them into tidy tables in a **warehouse**. Collection goes through a stream so the apps never wait.

The trade-off: raw data is flexible but messy — without catalogues and processing it becomes a "data swamp".

challenges.brief:
A law firm's knowledge base has two million documents. Keyword search finds "termination clause" but not "ending the contract early". The lawyers want search by meaning — while still finding exact case numbers and names.

tradeoff.q: Why combine keyword and vector search instead of using vectors alone?

Vectors capture meaning but blur exact tokens like case numbers and names; keywords catch those. Merging both rankings gives the best of each.
Keyword search is cheaper, so it should always be used alone.
tradeoff.why: Hybrid search costs two indexes and a merge step, and consistently beats either method alone on real queries.

challenges.learn:
**Semantic search**: an **embedding worker** turns document chunks into vectors stored in a **vector index**; queries are embedded the same way and matched by similarity. **Hybrid search** merges that with a keyword **search index**.

The trade-off: embedding costs compute, vectors take lots of memory, and the two rankings must be merged.

challenges.title: Who's online
challenges.brief:
A team-chat app shows a green dot next to people who are online. Today it writes "online" to the database on connect and "offline" on disconnect — but phones that lose signal never disconnect cleanly, so people look online for days.

estimate.q: How many heartbeat writes per second at peak?
estimate.workings: 5,000,000 / 30 s ≈ 166,667 writes/s — why presence lives in memory with a TTL, not in the database.

tradeoff.q: Why a TTL instead of writing "offline" on disconnect?
choices: TTLs are faster to read.
Clients often vanish without disconnecting; a key that expires when heartbeats stop is correct even when the goodbye never arrives.
Disconnects can't be detected at all.
tradeoff.why: TTL-based presence tolerates crashes and lost signal. The trade-off is a delay of up to one TTL before someone shows offline, and constant heartbeat traffic.

**Presence** = heartbeats + TTL: every 30 s the client's gateway refreshes a key in a fast key-value store with a 60 s TTL; if heartbeats stop, the key expires. Changes are fanned out to teammates' gateways via **pub/sub**.

The trade-off: presence is approximate (up to a TTL late) and heartbeats cost steady write load.

A delivery platform has 100,000 drivers on the road, each sending a GPS position every 4 seconds. The dispatch system must answer "which available drivers are within 2 km of this restaurant?" in milliseconds.

Geo indexes are more accurate.
tradeoff.why: Spatial indexes trade update cost (moving drivers between cells) for fast lookups. With 25,000 moves per second, keep the index in memory.

The trade-off: the index holds only the latest position and is slightly behind reality; history goes to cheaper storage for analytics.

challenges.brief:
A search start-up needs to crawl a billion pages a month. Each fetched page yields dozens of links, most already seen. DNS lookups for every URL are slow, and hammering one site with parallel requests gets the crawler banned.

A crawler is a loop: **frontier queue** → **fetchers** → store the page → extract links → **dedup** (Bloom filter) → back into the frontier. **Cached DNS** and **per-site rate limits** keep it fast and polite.

The trade-offs: the Bloom filter occasionally skips a page, and politeness caps how fast any one site is crawled.

The trade-off is complexity and storage for precomputed timelines, in exchange for instant reads.

The trade-off across all of them: eventual consistency (thumbnails and counts appear a moment later) for speed and scale.

All messages of a conversation land in one partition, so they keep their order, while different conversations are processed in parallel.
Partitions encrypt messages.
tradeoff.why: Per-conversation ordering is what users notice. The cost: a very busy group chat is limited to one partition's throughput.

challenges.learn:
Chat = **WebSocket gateways** for live connections, a **chat service** that stores each message (a wide-column store keyed by conversation) and publishes it to a **stream partitioned by conversation**, a **presence/session store** to find the recipients' gateways, and **push** for offline users. Receipts are just more messages on the same path.

The trade-off is state everywhere: connections, sessions and ordering all need care when gateways fail.

rules.text: Clients connect through a load balancer to several WebSocket gateways
rules.hint: Long-lived connections.

rules.text: Messages are stored before they are delivered
rules.hint: The chat service writes each message durably.

rules.text: Messages reach the recipients' gateways through a stream or topic
rules.hint: Gateway → chat → stream → gateway.

rules.text: Each conversation's messages stay in order
rules.hint: Partition the stream by conversation.

rules.text: The system knows who is online and on which gateway
rules.hint: A fast session store.

rules.text: Offline users get push notifications
rules.hint: Via a push service.

rules.text: Photos and files go to object storage
rules.hint: Don't put attachments in the message store.

rules.text: The load balancer works at L4
rules.hint: Connections last hours.

challenges.title: Video streaming
challenges.brief:
A documentary streaming service wants viewers on trains, sofas and cinemas-at-home to press play and never see buffering. Videos are uploaded by partner studios, then prepared for every screen and connection. Most views are of new releases; the back catalogue is rarely watched.

Design the path from studio upload to smooth playback anywhere.
functional: Studios upload masters
Videos are prepared in many bitrates, cut into segments
Viewers browse the catalogue and play
nonFunctional: Playback adapts to the viewer's connection
Segments come from servers near the viewer
Old masters cost little to keep

estimate.q: What is the peak outbound bandwidth?
estimate.workings: 1,000,000 viewers × 5 Mbps = 5,000,000 Mbps = 5 Tbps — only a CDN can deliver that.

tradeoff.q: Why cut video into short segments at several bitrates?
choices: Segments compress better.
The player can switch bitrate every few seconds as the connection changes, and segments are small, cacheable files a CDN serves well.
Studios require it.
tradeoff.why: Adaptive bitrate trades storage (6 renditions of everything) and transcoding time for smooth playback on any connection.

challenges.learn:
Streaming = **upload → queue → transcoders** producing **segments at several bitrates** plus a manifest → **object storage** → **CDN**. The player picks a bitrate per segment (**adaptive bitrate**). Masters move to a cold tier after release.

The trade-off: storage and transcoding multiply per rendition — the price of never buffering.

rules.text: Studios upload masters straight to storage
rules.hint: Huge files skip the app servers.

rules.text: Each upload queues transcoding jobs
rules.hint: Storage event or catalogue → queue → transcoders.

rules.text: Several transcoders write renditions back to storage
rules.hint: Many bitrates per video.

rules.text: Viewers stream segments through a CDN
rules.hint: Five terabits per second.

rules.text: Viewers browse a catalogue service
rules.hint: Titles, artwork, manifests.

rules.text: Segments are cached at the edge for a long time
rules.hint: Segments never change once written.

rules.text: Old masters move to a cheaper tier
rules.hint: Masters are needed only to re-transcode.

challenges.title: File sync
challenges.brief:
A file-sync service keeps a folder identical on a user's laptop, phone and tablet. Editing one slide in a 200 MB presentation shouldn't re-upload 200 MB, many users store the same files, and other devices should update within seconds of a change.

Design upload, storage, metadata and change notification.
functional: Upload changed parts of files
Keep version history
Other devices learn about changes and download them
nonFunctional: Only changed chunks are uploaded
Identical chunks are stored once
Devices see changes within seconds

estimate.q: With 30% of chunks being duplicates, how much storage does deduplication save?
estimate.workings: 1 PB = 1,000 TB × 30% = 300 TB saved; 700 TB actually stored.

tradeoff.q: Why name chunks by the hash of their content?
choices: Hashes are shorter than file names.
Identical content gets the same name, so the server can say "already have it" and skip the upload, and chunks can be verified on download.
Hashes make files load faster in editors.
tradeoff.why: Content addressing makes dedup and integrity checks natural. The trade-off: deleting data needs reference counting, because a chunk may belong to many files.

challenges.learn:
File sync splits files into **chunks named by hash**. The client asks the **metadata service** which chunks are new (a **dedup store** of known hashes), uploads only those straight to **object storage**, and commits a new file version. A change event reaches the other devices over **WebSockets**.

The trade-off is bookkeeping — chunk reference counts, version history and conflict copies when two devices edit offline.

rules.text: Devices commit file versions to a metadata service
rules.hint: Folders, files, versions and chunk lists.

rules.text: The metadata service knows which chunks already exist
rules.hint: A store of chunk hashes.

rules.text: Devices upload chunks straight to storage with signed URLs
rules.hint: Bytes skip the servers.

rules.text: Changes are published to other devices
rules.hint: Metadata → stream or topic → WebSocket gateways.

rules.text: Devices keep a live connection for change notices
rules.hint: Devices connect to the gateways.

rules.text: Sleeping phones get a push notification
rules.hint: Phones drop connections to save battery.

rules.text: Old versions move to a cheaper tier
rules.hint: Version history grows forever.

challenges.title: Ride sharing
challenges.brief:
A ride-sharing app matches riders with nearby drivers. Drivers stream their positions; a rider requests a ride and should see a driver accept within seconds. A driver must never be assigned two rides at once, and a finished trip is charged exactly once.

Design location, matching, trips and payment.
functional: Drivers report positions
Riders request rides and get matched to a nearby driver
Trips are tracked and charged at the end
nonFunctional: Match within seconds
A driver is never double-assigned
Each trip is charged once
Riders and drivers get live updates

numbers.label: Ride requests per second at peak

estimate.q: How many location updates per second?
estimate.workings: 300,000 drivers / 4 s = 75,000 updates per second.

tradeoff.q: Two riders' requests pick the same nearest driver at the same moment. What prevents a double assignment?
choices: Nothing; the driver will choose.
Assigning is a conditional write — "set driver busy only if still free" — using a lock or optimistic check, so only one assignment succeeds and the other retries with the next driver.
Sending both requests to the driver is fine.
tradeoff.why: Matching reads eventually consistent positions but must commit assignments strongly. The loser of the race simply tries the next-nearest driver.

challenges.learn:
Ride sharing combines a **location pipeline** (stream → **geo index**), a **matching service** that queries nearby drivers and commits the assignment with **locking**, a **trips** store, **idempotent payments**, and **push/WebSocket** updates.

The trade-off: positions are slightly stale, so matching must verify and lock before committing.

rules.text: Driver positions flow through a stream into a geo index
rules.hint: Location service → stream → consumer → geo index.

rules.text: Matching finds nearby drivers in the geo index
rules.hint: The matching service queries the index.

rules.text: A driver can only be assigned once
rules.hint: Locking on the trips database, or a distributed lock.

rules.text: Trips are stored by the trips service
rules.hint: Trip state lives somewhere durable.

rules.text: Trips are charged once through the payment provider
rules.hint: Idempotent payments service.

rules.text: Riders and drivers get live updates
rules.hint: Push or WebSocket.

rules.text: Payment calls retry safely and back off
rules.hint: Retries with jitter and a breaker.

rules.text: Positions are partitioned by driver
rules.hint: Keep each driver's updates in order.

challenges.title: Hotel booking
challenges.brief:
A hotel-booking site lets travellers search hotels by city, dates and filters, then book a room. Searches outnumber bookings a thousand to one. Search results may be slightly behind; a confirmed booking must never be double-booked.

Design search, availability, booking, payment and confirmation.
functional: Search hotels by city, dates and filters
Hold a room during checkout
Book and pay
Receive a confirmation email
nonFunctional: Search under 300 ms
No room is ever double-booked
Holds expire on their own if checkout is abandoned

estimate.q: How many bookings per day?
estimate.workings: 20M searches / 1,000 = 20,000 bookings per day — searches are the scale problem, bookings the correctness problem.

tradeoff.q: Why can search show slightly stale availability while booking can't?
choices: Search results don't matter.
Search is a read-optimised copy updated from changes; the booking step re-checks and locks the real inventory, so a stale search result only means an occasional "sorry, just taken".
Booking never reads availability.
tradeoff.why: Splitting the fast, approximate read path from the strict write path is what makes both scale. The cost is the rare disappointment at checkout.

challenges.learn:
Booking systems split **search** (a search index fed by **CDC**, cached, eventually consistent) from **booking** (a transaction with **locking** on real inventory, short **holds** that expire via TTL), then **payment** and an async **confirmation**.

The trade-off: search can be a moment behind, so checkout must re-verify.

rules.text: Searches are answered from a search index
rules.hint: Traveller → gateway → search service → index.

rules.text: The index is fed from inventory changes
rules.hint: CDC from the inventory database.

rules.text: Bookings are written by the booking service
rules.hint: The real inventory.

rules.text: A room can't be booked twice
rules.hint: Locking on the inventory database.

rules.text: Rooms are held briefly during checkout
rules.hint: Holds that expire by themselves: a key-value store with a TTL.

rules.text: Payment goes through the payments service
rules.hint: Booking → payments → provider.

rules.text: Confirmation emails are sent asynchronously
rules.hint: Queue → worker → email provider.

rules.text: Popular searches are cached
rules.hint: Many travellers search the same city and dates.

rules.text: Payments are idempotent
rules.hint: A retried checkout must not charge twice.

challenges.title: Job scheduler
challenges.brief:
A platform team is building a shared job scheduler: teams register millions of jobs ("every day at 02:00", "in 15 minutes"), and the scheduler must run each one on time — surviving machine failures, never silently skipping a job, and never running one twice in a way that matters.

Design job storage, triggering, dispatch and execution.
functional: Register one-off and recurring jobs through an API
Trigger jobs when due
Run them on workers and record results
nonFunctional: No single point of failure in triggering
A due job is never skipped
Failed jobs are retried, then parked
Duplicate runs are harmless

numbers.label: Share due at the top of the hour

estimate.q: If 40% of 10M daily runs are due at the 24 top-of-hour minutes, how many jobs are dispatched in that minute?
estimate.workings: 10M × 0.4 = 4M jobs / 24 hours ≈ 166,667 jobs in a single minute — why dispatch goes through a queue.

tradeoff.q: Why dispatch jobs through a queue rather than having the scheduler call workers directly?
choices: Queues run jobs faster.
The queue absorbs the top-of-the-hour burst, retries failures, parks poison jobs, and lets workers scale independently of the scheduler.
Workers can't receive calls.
tradeoff.why: The leader only decides *what* is due; the queue handles *delivery*. At-least-once delivery means workers must be idempotent.

challenges.learn:
A reliable scheduler: jobs in a **database**, several **schedulers** with **leader election** so exactly one scans for due jobs, a **queue** with **at-least-once** delivery, **retries** and a **DLQ**, and **idempotent workers**.

The trade-off: at-least-once means duplicates are possible, so every job must tolerate running twice.

rules.text: Teams register jobs through an API
rules.hint: Jobs are stored durably.

rules.text: Several schedulers elect a single leader
rules.hint: At least two schedulers with leader election on a coordination service.

rules.text: The scheduler reads due jobs
rules.hint: Schedulers read the jobs table.

rules.text: Due jobs are dispatched through a queue to workers
rules.hint: Scheduler → queue → workers.

rules.text: A dispatched job is never lost
rules.hint: At-least-once delivery.

rules.text: Failed jobs are retried, then parked
rules.hint: Retries and a dead-letter queue.

rules.text: Duplicate runs are harmless
rules.hint: Idempotent workers.

rules.text: Workers record results
rules.hint: Teams want to see when a job last ran.

rules.text: Parked jobs raise an alert
rules.hint: Someone must look at the DLQ.

challenges.title: Rate limiter service
challenges.brief:
A cloud company wants one rate-limiting service shared by all its public APIs: per-customer limits like "1,000 requests per minute, bursts of 100", enforced across dozens of gateway instances, adding at most a couple of milliseconds per request.

Design the limiter, where its counters live, and what happens when that store is slow.
functional: Enforce per-customer limits across all gateway instances
Allow short bursts within the limit
Limits are configurable per customer and API
nonFunctional: Adds under 2 ms per request
A slow or failed counter store never takes the APIs down
Counters survive a cache node failure

numbers.label: Ops per second one cache node handles

estimate.q: Each request does one counter operation. How many cache nodes (shards) are needed at minimum?
estimate.workings: 200,000 ops/s / 100,000 ops/s per node = 2 nodes, before adding replicas for failure.

tradeoff.q: The counter store times out. Should the limiter allow or block the request?
choices: Block — safety first, always.
Usually allow ("fail open") so a limiter problem doesn't become an outage for every customer, while alerting and falling back to rough local limits.
Retry until the store answers.
tradeoff.why: Failing open risks letting a burst through; failing closed turns a cache hiccup into a total outage. Most public APIs fail open with a local fallback.

challenges.learn:
A shared rate limiter uses a **token bucket** (limits plus bursts) with counters in a **replicated in-memory store**, called with a **tight timeout**, and a deliberate **fail-open** rule. Limit rules come from a config store and are cached.

The trade-off: an extra hop on every request, and a small risk of over-admitting when the store is unhealthy.

rules.text: Every API request passes the limiter at the gateway
rules.hint: Gateway → rate limiter.

rules.text: The gateway fronts several APIs
rules.hint: Shared by many APIs.

rules.text: Limits allow short bursts
rules.hint: Token bucket.

rules.text: Counters live in a shared in-memory store
rules.hint: Every gateway instance must see the same counters.

rules.text: Counter lookups time out in milliseconds
rules.hint: Set a tight timeout (≤ 20 ms) on the limiter's connection to the store.

rules.text: Counters survive a cache node failure
rules.hint: Replicas for the counter store.

rules.text: Limit rules come from a config store
rules.hint: Per-customer limits are data, not code.

rules.text: The limiter itself runs as more than one instance
rules.hint: Don't make it a single point of failure.

challenges.title: Food delivery, worldwide
challenges.brief:
A food-delivery company is launching on three continents at once. Customers order from restaurants, couriers are matched by location, and payments go through a global provider. Each city's traffic should stay in its nearest region, and a whole region may fail without affecting the others.

Design the platform — secure, observable, resilient, fast everywhere — and keep it within a budget of 70. Over-provisioning is the easy way to fail this one.
functional: Customers browse menus and order
Couriers are matched to orders by location
Payments are taken once per order
Customers and couriers get live notifications
nonFunctional: Users are served from the nearest of three regions
A region outage stays in that region
Only authenticated requests reach services
Payments never double-charge
Stay within a budget of 70

estimate.q: If orders are split evenly across three regions, how many orders per second does each region handle on average?
estimate.workings: 6,000,000 / 86,400 s ≈ 69 per second in total; / 3 regions ≈ 23 per second each.

tradeoff.q: Why keep each city's orders in its own region instead of one global database?
choices: Global databases can't store orders.
Orders are local by nature; keeping them in the nearest region makes reads and writes fast and lets a region fail alone. Only a little data (accounts, payments) is truly global.
It is cheaper to copy every order to every region.
tradeoff.why: Partitioning by geography gives local latency and independent failure at the cost of harder cross-region features (a customer ordering abroad). Replicating each region to a neighbour covers disaster recovery.

challenges.learn:
The capstone combines everything: **geo routing** to three regions, each with an **authenticating gateway**, **orders** and **courier** services, a local database and **geo index**, and an **event stream** between them; global **identity**, **payments** with idempotency and safe retries, a **CDN** for menus, **push** notifications and **alerting**.

The final trade-off is **cost**: spend on what the requirements demand, keep everything else lean.

rules.text: Users are routed to the nearest region
rules.hint: Geo DNS.

rules.text: Users sign in, and every region's gateway validates tokens
rules.hint: Identity provider plus authenticating gateways in three regions.

rules.text: Each region runs its own orders service and database
rules.hint: Orders stay local.

rules.text: Each region matches couriers from a local geo index
rules.hint: Couriers service → geo index, in every region.

rules.text: New orders reach courier matching through events
rules.hint: Orders → stream → couriers.

rules.text: Payments are idempotent and retried safely
rules.hint: Idempotent orders service; retries with backoff and jitter on the provider call.

rules.text: Stays within the budget of 70
rules.hint: Spend where the requirements demand it; keep the rest lean.

rules.text: Menus and photos come from a CDN
rules.hint: Static content at the edge.

rules.text: Customers and couriers get push notifications
rules.hint: Couriers service → push.

rules.text: Services report metrics and problems are paged
rules.hint: Metrics → alerting.

rules.text: Each region's orders are replicated to a neighbour
rules.hint: Disaster recovery without a fourth region.
